own_scenes.desc: El punk empieza en Inglaterra en 1975-76 y llega a California cuatro años después; de él sale el hardcore, fuerte en ambas costas estadounidenses y muy parecido al thrash naciente. Su código es el contrario del heavy: cualquiera puede tocar, voz plana sin emoción, igualdad entre fans y músicos frente a los guitar heroes. Grupos como los Misfits, llamados indistintamente horror metal y horror punk, muestran que la mezcla es posible; el thrash será un bricolage de segundo orden entre ambos códigos contradictorios.

refs.q: This emphasis on skill contrasts with the punk code, which emphasizes the simplicity of playing
refs.para: The style of play owes much to blues-based guitarists who transformed the urban blues–guitar sound into rock. Following the blues-rock tradition, heavy metal guitarists are required to demonstrate technical proficiency. This emphasis on skill contrasts with the punk code, which emphasizes the simplicity of playing, the idea that “hey, anybody can do this, I just learned it two weeks ago.” Punk stresses a leveling between fans and performers; heavy metal, with its guitar heroes, emphasizes distance.
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Heavy metal: la bestia que se niega a morir

refs.q: Groups such as the Misfits, which was alternately called a horror-metal band and a horror-punk band, showed the possibilities for a blending of punk and metal.
refs.para: Speed/thrash was most directly influenced by NWOBHM groups, such as Venom, Diamond Head, and Iron Maiden, all of which made rhythmic innovations. But it also followed in a line already present in heavy metal’s golden age. Moreover, speed/thrash bears the trace of the punk explosion. Punk began in England in 1975–76 and reached California four years later. It spawned hardcore, which was particularly strong on both coasts of the United States and bore many resemblances to the erupting speed/thrash style. Groups such as the Misfits, which was alternately called a horror-metal band and a horror-punk band, showed the possibilities for a blending of punk and metal. A more direct influence of hardcore entered the subgenre beginning in 1985–86, when groups such as DRI (Dirty Rotten Imbeciles) and Suicidal Tendencies created a style within a style, termed “thrashcore” or “crossover.”⁶⁶ Its traces reinforced the punk-related elements that were already present in the subgenre.

own_scenes.desc: El «Año Cero»: hacia el verano de 1977 el punk ya era una parodia de sí mismo y su frágil alianza entre chicos obreros y bohemios de escuela de arte se rompe. De un lado quedan los «punks verdaderos», populistas, que desembocarán en el Oi! y el hardcore; del otro, la vanguardia que se llamará postpunk, que vio en 1977 no un retorno al rock crudo sino la ocasión de romper con la tradición. Su legado común: la fe en el poder de la música y el «hazlo tú mismo».

notes.chapter: Cap. 1: Mi imagen pública me pertenece: John Lydon y PiL
notes.text: Never Mind the Bollocks (28 de octubre de 1977) fue para muchos la sentencia de muerte del punk: pura mercancía, un hard rock ortodoxo producido por Chris Thomas. Jon Savage lo sintió «como una lápida, sofocante, sin ningún espacio en la música»: le faltaba dub.

notes.chapter: Cap. 15: Sex Gang Children: Malcolm McLaren, el flautista de Hamelin del pantomime pop
notes.text: Muerto Sid Vicious y perdido el juicio con Lydon, McLaren ve cómo Virgin explota el cadáver de los Sex Pistols con singles póstumos, Some Product: Carri On y Flogging a Dead Horse: la crítica situacionista del consumismo convertida en producto.

refs.q: Hacia el verano de 1977, el punk se había convertido en una parodia de sí mismo
refs.para: Alfen Ravenstine, Pere Ubu, 1978 Hacia el verano de 1977, el punk se había convertido en una parodia de sí mismo. Muchos de los integrantes originales del movimiento sentían que algo cargado de posibilidades y de múltiples alternativas había degenerado en mera fórmula comercial. O peor aún, había demostrado ser una inyección rejuvenecedora para la industria musical establecida que los punks habían tenido la esperanza de derrocar.

refs.q: De un lado quedaron los "punks verdaderos", populistas
refs.para: Fue en este momento cuando comenzó a fracturarse la frágil unidad que el punk había forjado entre chicos de procedencia obrera y bohemios arty de clase media. De un lado quedaron los "punks verdaderos", populistas (que, después, habrían de evolucionar hacia los movimientos Oi! y hardcore), que creían que la música debía mantenerse accesible y sin pretensiones, como para seguir cumpliendo su rol de vocera de la rabia de las calles. Del otro lado estaba la vanguardia que habría de conocerse como postpunk, que encontró en 1977 no un rerorno al rock crudo, sino la oportunidad de establecer una ruptura con la tradición.

refs.q: como una lápida, sofocante, sin ningún espacio en la música
refs.para: El periodista Jon Savage hizo la crítica de Bollocks para la revista Sounds y hoy recuerda haberlo sentido "como una lápida, sofocante, sin ningún espacio en la música", un comentario que ubica el fracaso del disco en su carencia de dub. En comparación con la producción del reggae -pura neblina de reverbs centelleantes, efectos desorientadores e intermitentes volutas ectoplasmáticas-, la gran mayoría de los discos de punk sonaban simplemente retrógrados, atascados a mediados de los monocromáticos sesenta en mono, varados en algún lugar anterior a la paleta tímbrica ampliada y la brujería estereofónica de la psicodelia. Las bandas más perspicaces de todas aquellas que venían originalmente del punk sabían que tenían mucho por hacer para ponerse al día. Algunas de ellas, como The Clash y The Ruts, tomaron principalmente el aspecto de protesta del roots reggae: las consignas lanzadas abiertamente y el sermoneo de "Get Up Stand Up" de los Wailers y el chic radical del personaje de guerrillero rasta de Peter Tosh. En el extremo opuesto, las bandas postpunk más aventureras reaccionaron al reggae como si este fuera una revolución puramente sonora, una psicodelia africanizada que metamorfoseaba los contornos y alteraba la percepción. Durante la media década que va de 1977 a 1981, fueron exactamente la producción espacializada y los ritmos sofisticados pero elementales del reggae los que sentaron la base para todas las bandas postpunk que buscaban experimentar.

similar_scenes.name: Los primeros discos de ácido
similar_scenes.book: 1966: The Year the Decade Exploded
similar_scenes.author: Jon Savage
similar_scenes.desc: «The Third Eye» de los Dovers (abril de 1966) es uno de los primeros intentos de reproducir el viaje de LSD en un disco y de los más exactos: fanfarria oriental, drones a lo Ravi Shankar, doce cuerdas de raga, melodía horizontal sin cambios de acorde, voz de «místico punk» y una espiral casi fuera de control. Dura 135 segundos pero condensa una experiencia de ocho horas. Grupo de instituto de Santa Bárbara que había hecho folk rock en Gold Star, se rehízo a comienzos de 1966 animado a «viajar por el bien de la banda»; el guitarrista Bruce Clawson tradujo su asombro y su terror en un formato pop. El título viene del best seller de Lobsang Rampa (en realidad Cyril Hoskin, de Devon), que también usaron Dylan y los 13th Floor Elevators de Austin, formados expresamente para difundir la conciencia LSD. Aquellos primeros discos de ácido no eran beatíficos sino crudos, salvajes y amenazantes: «The Trip» de Kim Fowley, «Ain’t It Hard» de los Gypsy Trips, «Free Advice» de The Great!! Society!!. Sin una gran discográfica detrás, «The Third Eye» cayó en el vacío, y Clawson oyó «Eight Miles High» en la radio unas semanas después.

similar_scenes.name: Los rockers de garaje
similar_scenes.book: 1966: The Year the Decade Exploded
similar_scenes.author: Jon Savage
similar_scenes.desc: En 1966 no tenían nombre (Billboard los llamaba «rockers»); hoy se les llama grupos de garaje. La respuesta creativa americana a la invasión británica: chicos blancos de suburbio que ensayaban en el garaje familiar y tocaban en gimnasios, iglesias y fiestas, con cortes de pelo de Brian Jones, actitud de Jagger, fuzz, rave-ups a lo Yardbirds, Them y Stones y, casi siempre, un órgano Farfisa o Vox con un regusto siniestro de película de terror de autocine. Recuperaban la línea del rock americano de 1963-1964 (Kingsmen, Trashmen) que los Beatles cortaron en seco: «Hanky Panky» de Tommy James, grabado en 1963, fue número 1 en julio de 1966. Ese septiembre las listas se llenaron de discos duros: «96 Tears» de ? and the Mysterians (mexicanoamericanos de Flint, con un órgano hipnótico de otro disco), «Dirty Water» de los Standells, «You’re Gonna Miss Me» de los 13th Floor Elevators y «Psychotic Reaction» de Count Five, calco del «I’m a Man» de los Yardbirds. Quejas dirigidas a las mujeres, pero también una nueva confianza; quejas pequeñas que empezaban a encontrar un objetivo, como en «One of These Days» de los Roosters.
similar_scenes.family: Garage y punk americano

similar_scenes.name: Downtown: graffiti, punk y hip hop en el Mudd Club, Negril y el Roxy
similar_scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
similar_scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
similar_scenes.desc: Fab 5 Freddy (Fred Brathwaite), del grupo de grafiteros de Brooklyn Fabulous 5 con Lee Quiñones, ofrecía en The Village Voice murales por encargo; con Michael Holman montó la Canal Zone Party (1979), donde apareció Jean-Michel Basquiat, mitad de SAMO, y llevó a Bambaataa al Mudd Club. La Zulu Nation y los Funky 4 + 1, que mezclaban punk y hip hop ante los Beastie Boys, bajaron al Ritz, el Mudd Club, Danceteria, Negril y el Roxy de Kool Lady Blue: en Negril, cedido por el mánager de los Clash, se juntaron por primera vez los cuatro elementos; en el Roxy, una pista de patinaje de la calle 18, Bambaataa, Afrika Islam y Grand Mixer D.ST pinchaban para Bianca Jagger, Warhol, la Rock Steady Crew o Madonna. Debbie Harry y Chris Stein (Blondie), amigos de Flash, nombraron a Freddy y a Flash en «Rapture» (1981), primer rap número 1 en Billboard, y llevaron a los Funky 4 + 1 a Saturday Night Live (14 de febrero de 1981), primera actuación de hip hop en la televisión nacional. Para Holman, sin el abrazo del downtown el hip hop no habría sido lo que fue; para Dante Ross, los negros se llevaron pantalones pitillo y opiáceos y los blancos toda esa cultura.

similar_scenes.name: Rick James
similar_scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
similar_scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
similar_scenes.desc: James Ambrose Johnson Jr., criado por su madre en Búfalo, recadero de apuestas a los quince, desertor de la marina, huido a Canadá y Londres, llevó a Motown un funk sucio, intenso y peligroso. El primero en quitarle la corona a P-Funk, con sexo, drogas e irresponsabilidad: «You and I», «Mary Jane», «Bustin’ Out», «Love Gun». Street Songs (1981), su cima: «Give It to Me Baby» definió la nueva guarrería del R&B y fue el principio del fin; «Super Freak», de ritmo new wave (base de «U Can’t Touch This» de MC Hammer), el dúo «Fire and Desire» con Teena Marie y crónica callejera como «Ghetto Life» o «Mr. Policeman», que anticipaba el gangsta rap. Su Stone City Band mantuvo los solos de viento. Luego «Standing on the Top», «Cold Blooded», las Mary Jane Girls («All Night Long») y la caída, hasta la cárcel de Folsom.

similar_scenes.name: Punk neoyorquino del CBGB
similar_scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
similar_scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
similar_scenes.desc: Ramones, Television, Patti Smith, Blondie, The Heartbreakers: una escena que, como advirtió James Wolcott en 1975 («Un impulso conservador en el nuevo underground del rock»), se presentaba como el retorno de algo perdido. Los Ramones agotan su idea en dos discos, los Heartbreakers son Dr. Feelgood con heroína y hasta Television bebe del acid rock de la costa oeste. La revista Punk de Legs McNeil proclama «¡Muerte a esa mierda disco!» y rechaza al hipster como «negro blanco».

similar_scenes.name: Industrial y acid punk de San Francisco
similar_scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
similar_scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
similar_scenes.desc: La tercera edad dorada de la bohemia de San Francisco: Factrix quería «llevar el teatro de la crueldad al rock» con instrumentos modificados (el Optigan tocado al revés), percusión africana programada y la guitarra lisérgica de Bond Bergland, «discípulos del feedback». Con Monte Cazazza y los robots de Mark Pauline (Survival Research Laboratories) montan espectáculos como Night of the Succubus (1981). Chrome, de Damon Edge y Helios Creed, inventa un «acid punk» o cyberpunk de guitarra corrosiva tras escuchar Never Mind the Bollocks: Alien Soundtracks, Half Machine Lip Moves. También Z'ev y Nervous Gender, documentados por Subterranean en Live at Target.
similar_scenes.family: Industrial y electrónica

similar_scenes.name: Punk funk neoyorquino: 99 Records, ESG y Liquid Liquid
similar_scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
similar_scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
similar_scenes.desc: El sello de la tienda anglófila de Ed Bahlman, con producción más cruda que ZE: ESG, las hermanas Scroggins del Bronx, funk ultraminimalista («apenas algunos golpes con un par de palillos y una simple melodía de bajo»), que Tony Wilson graba con Martin Hannett («Moody», «UFO»), luego adoptado por el house y sampleado por el rap. Liquid Liquid, percusión latina del Lower East Side y Fela Kuti («Cavern», plagiada en «White Lines» de Grandmaster Flash). Bush Tetras de Pat Place («Too Many Creeps»: «ritmo y paranoia»), Y Pants y el single de Vivien Goldman con Keith Levene.

similar_scenes.name: Oi! y anarcopunk
similar_scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
similar_scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
similar_scenes.desc: Las dos derivas del punk que se tomaron en serio la explotación y la injusticia social: el Oi! o «punk de verdad» (The Exploited, Cockney Rejects, Garry Bushell en Sounds como ideólogo), protesta extrema arraigada en la clase obrera, a veces contaminada por la ultraderecha; y el anarcopunk de Crass y su sello, discos-panfleto contra el Estado, la Iglesia y el Ejército, a favor del pacifismo y la autonomía. El gótico nació en parte como reacción contra su «temática mundana».
similar_scenes.family: Antecedentes: punk, art rock, kraut y glam

similar_scenes.name: Gótico
similar_scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
similar_scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
similar_scenes.desc: Término que Hannett aplicó a Joy Division y luego insulto para los epígonos, hasta que en 1982 los fans lo adoptan como estandarte frente a la excesiva luminosidad del new pop: glamour sepulcral, retorno de lo reprimido, emociones atemporales. Bauhaus («Bela Lugosi's Dead», 1979, el comienzo propiamente dicho; Peter Murphy, sex symbol heredero de Adam Ant y Bowie), The Birthday Party (el gótico americano de Nick Cave: «Release the Bats», Junkyard), Killing Joke («música de tensión», del funk de PiL a Black Sabbath, con un aura inquietante), The Cure (gótico light: Seventeen Seconds, Faith, Pornography). El club The Batcave (1982), el «positive punk», Southern Death Cult, Theatre of Hate, The Sisters of Mercy («¡Nosotros sí somos una banda de rock!»), el death rock de Los Ángeles y Kukl con Björk. Su deriva: coqueteos totalitarios y la conversión en versión postpunk del heavy metal (The Cult).
similar_scenes.family: Mánchester, gótico y rock oscuro

similar_scenes.name: Punk-rock británico
similar_scenes.book: A History of Rock Music 1951-2000
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: La gira de los Ramones de 1976 contagia a Inglaterra, donde el punk es combinación de moda y paro: la Gran Bretaña de Thatcher, con las ciudades industriales devastadas, convierte el «punk» en algo mucho más serio que lo que pretendían los Ramones. Malcolm McLaren inventa el sonido (Sex Pistols, «los Ramones con heroína y valium») y la imagen. The Clash, los más intelectuales (London Calling, Sandinista); Damned, Generation X, Buzzcocks (inventores del punk-pop), Vibrators. En Australia, Radio Birdman y los Saints. La segunda ola (GBH, UK Subs, Neurotics, New Model Army, Stiff Little Fingers) y el punk anarquista (Crass, Discharge, Rudimentari Peni, Subhumans).
similar_scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

similar_scenes.name: Art-punk y funk-punk británico
similar_scenes.book: A History of Rock Music 1951-2000
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: Las bandas artísticas del primer punk: Wire (de Pink Flag a la desolación electrónica de 154), Colin Newman, The Fall de Mark E. Smith, los anárquicos Swell Maps, los Mekons, las Slits (primera banda punk femenina) y los australianos Birthday Party de Nick Cave. Muchos punks redescubren la esencia «salvaje» del jazz y el funk: Pop Group (Y, fusión catastrófica de primitivismo y futurismo con dub, funk y agit-prop), Rip Rig & Panic, Gang Of Four, A Certain Ratio y Wolfgang Press.
similar_scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

similar_scenes.name: Dark punk y rock gótico
similar_scenes.book: A History of Rock Music 1951-2000
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: El punk británico estuvo flanqueado desde el principio por un movimiento «gótico» que canalizaba su violencia hacia atmósferas de terror y rituales esotéricos: Stranglers, Siouxsie, X-Ray Spex. Lo más interesante evita el tono de película de terror: The Cure introducen la angustia existencial de Camus y Sartre (Pornography, Disintegration); Joy Division mezclan Doors, Kraftwerk y Black Sabbath y su final anuncia el synth-pop; Bauhaus, Killing Joke, Psychedelic Furs, los irlandeses Virgin Prunes y la cima del género, Public Image Ltd de Johnny Lydon, que convierte el punk en música de cámara con dub y ecos étnicos (Second Edition, Flowers Of Romance). Después, el gótico bailable de Sisters Of Mercy, Alien Sex Fiend, Cult, Mission e In The Nursery.
similar_scenes.family: Gótico e industrial

similar_scenes.name: Roots-rock de los ochenta y cow-punk
similar_scenes.book: A History of Rock Music 1951-2000
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: Como en 1970 tras 1966, la new wave de 1976 va seguida de un revival del roots-rock, esta vez gradual y disfrazado: punks que desfiguran los estilos tradicionales (X, Dream Syndicate, Gun Club) y los «cow-punks» que tocan country ambientado entre inadaptados: Long Ryders, Jason & The Scorchers, Fetchin Bones, Lone Justice, Beat Farmers. El populismo de Los Lobos, Del Fuegos, Del-Lords y Walkabouts; en la Costa Oeste, los dementes Camper Van Beethoven, Donner Party, Catheads, Thin White Rope y los American Music Club de Mark Eitzel; en Texas, Wild Seeds, Poi Dog Pondering, Glass Eye; en los Grandes Lagos, BoDeans, Soul Asylum, Afghan Whigs, Shrimp Boat y los canadienses Cowboy Junkies. Nashville se renueva con los neotradicionalistas (George Strait, Randy Travis, Garth Brooks, Lyle Lovett, Steve Earle, Dwight Yoakam) y el surf instrumental vuelve con Shadowy Men On A Shadowy Planet.
similar_scenes.family: Raíces: rock'n'roll, country y roots

similar_scenes.name: Cruces del punk: de Fugazi al punk-pop
similar_scenes.book: A History of Rock Music 1951-2000
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: A finales de los ochenta el punk es el más vivo de los subgéneros del rock: miles de bandas ensayando en garajes, un lenguaje universal como no se veía desde los sesenta. Nueva York: Adrenalin O.D., el straight-edge de Youth Of Today y Gorilla Biscuits, el crossover punk-metal (Cro-Mags, Prong, Danzig). Washington lanza a Pussy Galore (la irrelevancia hecha relevante), Unrest y Fugazi de Ian MacKaye, que abstrae el hardcore en una forma teatral de compromiso ético y estético (Repeater, Steady Diet Of Nothing, Red Medicine), y Royal Trux (Twin Infinitives, «un Trout Mask Replica para la generación grunge»). El punk-pop de Mr T Experience, Dwarves, Henry Rollins, L7 (pioneras del «foxcore»), Lemonheads, Screeching Weasel, Goo Goo Dolls, Fastbacks, Shonen Knife; el «rogue folk» de los Pogues, Membranes y Chumbawamba.
similar_scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

similar_scenes.name: Hardcore en la era del punk-pop: emocore, ska-core y post-hardcore
similar_scenes.book: A History of Rock Music 1951-2000
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: Mientras las revistas anuncian la «muerte del punk», el hardcore se convierte en un movimiento que no deja pueblo sin tocar y genera subgéneros. El «emocore» (Jawbreaker, Weezer, Sunny Day Real Estate, Promise Ring, At The Drive-In, Jimmy Eat World, Seaweed); el hardcore progresivo de Washington (Nation Of Ulysses, Make-Up, Shudder To Think, Jawbox, Edsel, Lungfish, Circus Lupus, Dismemberment Plan); el «ska-core» (Operation Ivy, Rancid, Mighty Mighty Bosstones, Sublime, No Doubt); el punk-pop que llega a las listas (Green Day, Offspring, Flop, Pennywise, Pegboy, Superchunk, Queers); el garage-punk californiano (Drive Like Jehu, Rocket From The Crypt, Blink 182, Zen Guerrilla); el jazzcore (Bazooka, Iceburn); la vieja escuela (D Generation, Supersuckers, Zeke, Dropkick Murphys, Silverfish, Turbonegro) y el post-hardcore de Unwound.
similar_scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

similar_scenes.name: Errorismo / Punk digital
similar_scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
similar_scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
similar_scenes.desc: La música experimental descubre las primeras computadoras y explota el error como fuente de una expresión bromista y provocadora.
similar_scenes.family: Vanguardia y experimental

similar_scenes.name: Post-punk dub (On-U Sound)
similar_scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
similar_scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
similar_scenes.desc: El punk, el funk y el dub se entretejen: el estudio como instrumento. The Slits con Dennis Bovell, The Pop Group en Bristol y, sobre todo, Adrian Sherwood y su sello On-U Sound: New Age Steppers, African Head Charge (precursor del techno-dub) y Tackhead, banda de estudio que endureció el sonido hacia el funk industrial y politizado.
similar_scenes.family: Jamaica y sound system

similar_scenes.name: Punk electrónico
similar_scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica

similar_scenes.desc: Tras el viaje de John Lydon a Jamaica nace el post-punk: PiL infecta de dub sus diatribas. El punk blanco se cruza con la música negra (A Certain Ratio, ESG, Liquid Liquid, Gang of Four, Shriekback, 23 Skidoo), Wire construye nuevos lenguajes, y Joy Division renace tras la muerte de Ian Curtis como New Order, que hermana post-punk y disco americana y prepara al Reino Unido para el house. Factory tuvo su propio club: The Haçienda.

podcast.title: "The Wild One" (1953) Influence
podcast.body: The 1953 movie "The Wild One," starring Marlon Brando as the leather-jacketed motorcycle rider Johnny Strombo, was a pivotal film in exploring American motorcycle gangs. This movie, and the attention it brought to the subculture, resurrected the older Victorian definition of a "punk" as a young criminal in the public consciousness. "The next step in the evolution of the word came with the release of a 1953 movie called The Wild One."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lester Banks' Early Print Usage (April 6, 1969)
podcast.body: Detroit rock writer Lester Banks made a significant early use of the word "punks" in a musical context in a review of an MC5 album. Published in Rolling Stone magazine on April 6, 1969, he described the group as "a bunch of 16-year-old punks on a meth power trip," helping to forge the connection between the term and rebellious rock music. "In a review of an album by a Detroit group called the MC5, published in Rolling Stone magazine on April the 6th of 1969, he managed to use this phrase. A bunch of 16-year-old punks on a meth power trip."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Uses in Music Criticism (1970-1971)
podcast.body: The term "punk" began appearing in music criticism in the early 1970s; Lester Bangs called Iggy Pop a "stooge punk" in Cream Magazine (December 1970), and Dave Marsh referred to Question Mark and the Mysterians as "purveyors of punk rock" in Cream (May 1971). Alan Vega's band Suicide also adopted the term for their "punk masses" gigs. "In December 1970, the Detroit-based music magazine called Cream ran an article from a critic named Lester Banks who referred to Iggy Pop as that stooge punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave Marsh Coins "Punk Rock" in Print (May 1971)
podcast.body: Writer Dave Marsh is credited with the first printed use of the phrase "punk rock" in May 1971. He used it in an article about the reformation of the 60s garage band Question Mark in the Mysterians, describing their reunion as "a landmark explosion of punk rock," a crucial moment in the term's evolution. "And the guy who seems to have done it first in print anyway was a writer named Dave Marsh."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early "Punk Rock" as an Aesthetic (1971)
podcast.body: In 1971, "punk rock" was understood more as an aesthetic or attitude than a defined sound, primarily used by writers and critics rather than musicians themselves. Early artists like Alice Cooper and Kiss were even considered "punk rock" by some, indicating the term's initial broad and somewhat unfocused application. "In 1971 punk rock was more of a aesthetic than a sound. It was a phrase used by writers and critics not musicians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Record Claim (1974)
podcast.body: Patti Smith's debut 1974 single, featuring an original song (likely "Piss Factory"), is regarded by many music historians as the "first true punk rock record," marking a pivotal moment in the genre's history.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Emergence in 1974
podcast.body: Punk rock was an emerging force in 1974, notably marked by the formation of The Ramones during that year.

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 48 - The Worst of the 70s The Music of 1974

podcast.title: Socio-economic Roots (1974)
podcast.body: The deconstruction of punk's origins begins in 1974, examining the socio-economic factors that served as a "great musical Big Bang" in history. "Let's start this deconstruction by looking at the socio-economic factors behind one of the great musical Big Bangs in history. And we're going to begin in 1974."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Global Germination (1975)
podcast.body: By 1975, punk rock had started "germinating" in New York, with significant contributions from the Cleveland music scene, indicating its early spread and development beyond a single geographical origin. "By 1975, punk rock had started germinating in New York, thanks to help from Cleveland."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Term Definition by "Punk" Magazine (1975)
podcast.body: The fanzine "Punk," launched at the end of 1975, was crucial in defining the term. It covered artists like Lou Reed, The Ramones, Iggy Pop, The Stooges, The New York Dolls, and 60s garage bands. Its name, inspired by The Dictators' 1975 album "Go Girl Crazy," solidified "punk" as the descriptor for the new, stripped-down rock and roll sound and the artists associated with the CBGB scene. "And so, the authors of this fanzine decided to call their publication, Punk. And as the CBGB scene grew bigger, circulation increased, and soon anyone who was featured in the fanzine was known as a punk artist."

podcast.title: The Rocky Horror Picture Show Costumes (1975)
podcast.body: The costumes designed by Sue Blaine for *The Rocky Horror Picture Show* in 1975, featuring wild multicolored hair, crazy makeup, and fishnet stockings, were noted for their punk rock aesthetic, emerging around the time punk was just beginning. Blaine claimed to have improvised the designs with a budget of only $1,600, possibly influencing early punk fashion. "Wild multicolored hair, crazy makeup, fishnet stockings. Did the movie influence the fashion of punk rock? Maybe."

podcast.title: "Great Explosion" of 1976
podcast.body: The year 1976 is identified as the "Great Punk Rock Explosion," a pivotal event from which nearly all modern alternative music originates, akin to a "big bang" for the genre. "Our starting point is 1976, the year of the Great Punk Rock Explosion, the thing from which practically all of today's alternative music emanates."

podcast.title: 1976 Explosion
podcast.body: The year 1976 is identified as the "big bang" or explosion of punk rock, which served as the foundational event leading to all subsequent alternative rock music. "We're picking 1976 as our starting year because that was the year of the punk rock explosion, the big bang that led to all the Alt Rock that followed."

podcast.title: 1976-1977 Seismic Shift
podcast.body: The birth and rise of punk in 1976 and 1977 are described as a seismic period in music history, paralleling the transformative years of alt-rock in 1990-1991. "They are every bit as seismic as what we saw with the birth and rise of punk in 1976 and 1977."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Adoption of "Punk" (Summer 1976)
podcast.body: British writers like Nick Kent and aspiring managers such as Malcolm McLaren discovered the nascent New York scene and eagerly adopted the term "punk." They imported it into the UK, where it coincided with the rise of bands like the Sex Pistols and The Clash, leading to the "British punk rock explosion" that began in the summer of 1976 and officially christened their movement "punk rock." "It wasn't long before British writers and scene stars happened upon what was going on in New York. And they really liked the word punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cultural Storm Example (1976-1982)
podcast.body: Punk Rock is cited as an example of a "perfect cultural storm," with its period of significant impact and influence spanning from 1976 to 1982. "Think of Punk Rock from 76 to 82."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Editorial Stance and Anti-Disco Sentiment (1976)
podcast.body: The first editorial of Punk magazine, published in January 1976, issued a provocative and defiant call to action. It famously urged readers to engage in extreme acts rather than listen to disco, emphasizing the magazine's role in guiding its audience towards a new musical and cultural sensibility. "Kill yourself, jump off a cliff, drive nails into your head, become a robot and join the staff at Disneyland, OD, anything. Just don't listen to disco, educate yourself, read punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5

podcast.title: English Rock Turning Point (1976)
podcast.body: The Sex Pistols' gig at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4, 1976, despite being a financial failure with fewer than 50 attendees, proved to be a pivotal turning point for English rock. The concert inspired future members of significant bands like the Buzzcocks, Pet Shop Boys, Joy Division, and New Order, sparking the widespread adoption and creation of punk rock across England. "Didn't seem like much of the time, but this failed money losing gig became a turning point for English rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5

podcast.title: Growth and Organization (1976)
podcast.body: By September 1976, hundreds of punk rock bands had formed across Britain, attracting regular followings and playing gigs wherever possible. This growth led to the organization of larger events, such as the 100 Club Punk Rock Festival, to assess the burgeoning scene. "Still, by September of 1976, there were hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of these punk rock bands all over Britain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Magazine Origin of the Term (1976)
podcast.body: The term "punk" was adopted as the name for the musical genre from a fanzine started by Legs McNeil and his friend in January 1976. The decision to name the magazine "Punk" was influenced by the album artwork of The Dictators, and it rapidly became the defining label for the new wave of hard, fast rock music emerging from New York. "So that is when legs and his buddy decided to call the magazine punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5

podcast.title: Punk Rock (1976) – Reactionary Not Revolutionary; Return to Short Sharp Songs; The Rock Great Schism
podcast.body: Punk rock emerged almost simultaneously in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia in 1976. It was a reactionary backlash against how complicated and artsy rock had become — a return to short, sharp, melodic songs, but faster, louder, more anti-establishment. The Ramones were the most important early spreaders of the gospel from 1974 onward. British punk was less artsy and more political, concerned with the class system. 1976 was to rock what the Great Schism of 1054 was to the Catholic Church — it split rock into two mostly independent and autonomous streams that ran parallel, crossing over only rarely, each disavowing the other. "It wasn't revolutionary at all. It was reactionary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shift from Curiosity to Mainstream Force (1976)
podcast.body: Before December 1st, 1976, punk rock was a "weird curiosity" confined to the fringes of the mainstream press. Following the Sex Pistols' infamous 117-second live TV interview on the *Today* show, the genre exploded into national conversation in the UK, becoming widely discussed, albeit often negatively. This controversy, however, fueled its popularity, transforming it into "the biggest and most dangerous thing in the world." "Suddenly the whole nation was talking about punk rock and how awful it was."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10

podcast.title: UK Scene (Fall 1976) – Concentrated London Festival
podcast.body: The UK punk scene emerged in the fall of 1976 with a similarly small number of participants. Nearly every London punk could fit into a single venue, the 100 Club on Oxford Street, which hosted a two-night music festival with an official capacity of 350, though there was reportedly ample space to move around. "The UK punk scene started with a similar number in the fall of 1976. Pretty much every London punk fit into a single club on Oxford Street for a two-night music festival."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1977 British Exposure
podcast.body: Thanks to the notoriety of the Sex Pistols, punk rock culture became widely exposed across Britain in 1977, leading to the emergence of hundreds of new punk groups. "Thanks to the notoriety of the Sex Pistols, all of Britain had been at least exposed to punk rock culture."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Characteristics and Industry Role (1977-1978)
podcast.body: Punk was characterized by a raw, fresh sound based on first takes, aggressive lyrics, and a technically incorrect approach to music. Its recording methods were often inherited from bands like Iggy Pop and Black Sabbath. In the UK, punk was strongly linked to anarchist political movements. By 1977-78, with the release of albums like the Sex Pistols' *Never Mind the Bollocks*, punk had become a highly lucrative business for record labels. "El punk tenia esa vertiente que era como muy fresca, se basaban las primeras tomas de grabación, era como muy agresivo, no era técnicamente correcto, tenía una manera grabar como muy heredada de otras bandas pues como podía ser hipólogo, como podía ser incluso Black Sabbath"

podcast.title: Death of Punk Sentiment (January 25, 1977)
podcast.body: The day The Clash signed a worldwide contract with CBS Records for 129,000 pounds on January 25, 1977, was considered by some of "Punk's hardcore adherence" as "the day Punk died." This sentiment arose despite the band's position that they intended to "subvert the record industry from within," as signing with a major label was seen as a betrayal of punk's anti-establishment ethos.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence from Rock (1977)
podcast.body: Punk music emerged from the rock side of popular music in 1977, following significant genre splits that created a lot of polarization. This new genre established an "incredible" and enduring legacy. "On the rock side, we got punk."

podcast.title: Emergence in 1977
podcast.body: The year 1977 is considered the beginning of punk rock, alongside New Wave and post-punk, marking a significant shift in music after the earlier prolific years of rock. "1977 punk, the beginning of New Wave, the era of post punk and all that came with it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rapid Musical Evolution in 1977
podcast.body: The rules for music underwent extremely rapid changes in 1977; indeed, it's more accurate to say that all established rules were quickly broken. This period opened up rock and roll to novel interpretations by a new generation. It was observed that rock is one of the rare art forms that can actually be enhanced by practitioners who are not technically skilled, suggesting that allowing passion to guide without adherence to rules can lead to wonderful outcomes. "The rules for music changed very fast in 1977. Actually it's probably more accurate to say that all the rules were broken very fast in 1977."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1978-1982 Music Industry Revolution
podcast.body: Between 1978 and 1982, the music industry underwent a revolution. This period was described as "very convulsive," with the punk movement still prominent ("estaba en la hoja del punk"). "estaba en la hoja del punk, eran momentos muy convulsos."

podcast.title: Avant-garde Faction (1978)
podcast.body: In 1978, another faction of punk emerged, described as "avant-garde." They believed the punk revolution could achieve more than just four-chord accelerated rock and roll songs, emphasizing that "form could be much more radical and revolutionary than the message." Unlike traditional punks who rejected the past, avant-garde punks looked to previous bands for inspiration. "Pero por otro lado, había otra facción ahora que vamos a llamar van guardista. Ellos me llan que la revolución punk podía servir para mucho más que hacer canciones con cuatro cordes acelerados de rock and roll."

podcast.title: Counterculture Development (1978-79)
podcast.body: During the "winter of discontent" (1978-79), exacerbated by widespread strikes and extreme cold, punk rock intensified, transforming "from being this innocuous sort of thing into a genuine counterculture." "All this simply increased the heat of punk. It went from being this innocuous sort of thing into a genuine counterculture."

podcast.title: Most Famous Punk Rock Hotel Room Death (October 12, 1978)
podcast.body: The death of Nancy Spungen at the Chelsea Hotel on October 12, 1978, is considered "probably the most famous punk rock hotel room death of them all." "And then there's probably the most famous punk rock hotel room death of them all."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Revolutionary Impact and Mainstream Presence by 1978
podcast.body: By 1978, punk music was in full swing, having already revolutionized the music industry since the 1976 releases by bands like the Sex Pistols. Other key bands like New York Dolls and Ramones had also emerged, making punk a strong influence on contemporary music, including The Rolling Stones' "Some Girls" album. "el panque estaba en pleno auge, ya había salido los New York 2, ya había sido los Ramones y en 1976 los expisto, la había reucinaró toda la industria musical."

podcast.title: Soviet Awareness and Interception (1978)
podcast.body: Soviet authorities became aware of punk rock in 1978 when bootleg tapes and news from legally intercepted BBC broadcasts began "dripping through the iron curtain." The KGB was conscious of this new music and its potential for social disruption and youth anger. "Soviet authorities first became aware of punk in 1978 when bootleg tapes and news were legally intercepted BBC broadcasts, started dripping through the iron curtain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Traditional Faction (1978)
podcast.body: In 1978, punk was divided, with a traditional faction largely composed of working-class individuals. They believed music should be noisy, stripped of artistic pretensions, based on accelerated rock and roll, and function as a "megaphone for the street." This branch later led to scenes like hardcore and the Oi! movement. "por un lado estaban los pános más tradicionales, gente por lo general de clase obrera, que creía que la música debía ser ruidosa y estar casi despojada de pretensiones artísticas."

srcs.source: Central Sonora

podcast.title: Burning Out by Early 1979
podcast.body: The original punk rock scene, which had ignited a new wave of music, had largely "burned itself out" by early 1979, paving the way for the emergence of the post-punk era. "By early 1979, the original punk rock scene had pretty much burned itself out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-1980 Continuation and Commercialization
podcast.body: After 1980, punk rock continued its presence, but it gradually became significantly dominated and influenced by multinational corporations. This marked a shift from its earlier independent origins, as it persisted as a stylistic remnant during the highly effervescent early 1980s musical landscape. "el punk continuó un poco más allá en 1980 pero ya fue dominado bastante por algunas multinacionales."

podcast.title: Times Square Soundtrack Introduction (1980)
podcast.body: The soundtrack for the 1980 movie *Time Square* was one of the very first to feature the nascent punk rock and new wave music of the day. Despite the movie and double LP's dismal sales, for those who purchased it, it offered an immediate look at cutting-edge music and significantly contributed to introducing people to these genres. "Time Square did a lot to introduce people to punk a new wave."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First MTV Punk Video (1981)
podcast.body: The Ramones' "Do You Remember Rock and Roll Radio?" was the first punk song video shown on MTV, appearing as the 105th video in the channel's initial library after its launch on August 1st, 1981. This marked punk rock's early representation on the new music video network. "And the first punk song was Do You Remember Rock and Roll Radio by the Ramones at number 105?"

podcast.body: By 1994, a new generation of "pure punk" bands, influenced by the Ramones, such as Offspring, Rancid, and Green Day, "overtook the modern rock and even the pop charts." This explosion of punk came too late for the original bands like The Ramones. "A new generation of what you might call pure punk of the Ramones variety, led by bands like Offspring, Rancid and Green Day overtook the modern rock and even the pop charts by 1994."

podcast.title: "FU to the Establishment" and Space for Women
podcast.body: Punk rock, which emerged by the end of the 1970s, was characterized as a "big FU to the establishment." This anti-establishment ethos created a space for women in the genre, offering a counter-cultural environment where female artists could thrive. "Punk was a big FU to the establishment. So it makes sense that there is space for women in the genre."

podcast.body: It is suggested that David Bowie's 1977 album and song "Heroes" might have been "too arty" for its time, given the prevalent music genres of the era, which included punk, disco, and arena rock. podcast.title: "Pop Punk" Emergence
podcast.body: By the time Blink-182 released "Enema of the State," "pop punk" had solidified its place as "a real thing with fans," indicating its mainstream appeal and commercial viability, aligning perfectly with the band's sound and attitude. "And pop punk had become a real thing with fans. So Blink had this right sound and this right attitude at exactly the right time."

podcast.title: "Punk Magazine" Influence
podcast.body: *Punk Magazine*, a New York-based publication, played a significant role in popularizing the underground music scene in New York City. It is suggested that the magazine may have even lent its name to the emerging music genre, solidifying the idea that if *Punk* wrote about a band, they were considered a "punk band." podcast.title: "Selling Out" Perception
podcast.body: In the punk rock community, profiting from music is often seen as fundamentally "wrong." This perspective emphasizes that money compromises ideals and principles, destroying the purity of the music and betraying the values shared between the artist and fan.

podcast.title: 1970s Origins as Revival
podcast.body: The original punk rock explosion in the mid-1970s was itself a revival, a "reactionary" movement that stripped rock back to its essence. It emerged as a response to the perceived excesses of prog rock, the detachment of stadium rock, and the blandness of AM radio music, re-emphasizing simplicity, attitude, and accessibility regardless of musical ability. "Punk rock was not revolutionary. It was in fact reactionary. Rock was stripped back to its essence in terms of instrumentation, arrangement, performance, and attitude."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1970s Punk Ethos Resurgence (1990s)
podcast.body: By 1990, a large demographic of young people, Generation X, was returning to the "punk ethos" of the 1970s. This movement emphasized authenticity, humbleness, and a breakdown of barriers between performers and audience, signifying a desire for music made by regular people, for regular people. "By 1990, this huge group of kids was returning to the punk ethos of the 1970s, where there were no barriers between the performer and the audience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1970s Special Time
podcast.body: The 1970s punk movement created a strong sense among its followers that it was a truly special and exciting time for music and for being alive. "If you were tied in with punk in the 1970s, there was a sense among you and your friends that this was a really special time for music and a good time to be alive."

podcast.title: 1990s Revival Factors
podcast.body: The punk rock revival of the 1990s was facilitated by several factors: the groundwork laid by grunge (which name-checked punk influences), the music industry's "herd mentality" to sign similar acts, the death of Kurt Cobain which shifted focus away from grunge, and a broader socio-economic climate of optimism (end of Cold War, economic recovery). "But more important was the herd mentality of the record industry. You know how it works. Once a successful trend is identified, there's a stampede to sign and promote acts for that space."

podcast.title: 1990s Revival Wave
podcast.body: Sum 41 emerged at the tail end of the punk rock revival of the 1990s, successfully catching this wave of popularity and leveraging it for their initial success. "You were part of sort of like the end of the punk rock revival of the 1990s."

podcast.title: 80s Alt-Rock Radio Inclusion
podcast.body: Various "conceivable flavors of punk" were among the diverse genres featured on alt-rock radio playlists in the 1980s, demonstrating the broad range of music played before the rise of grunge.

podcast.title: 924 Gilman Street Club – All-Ages Punk Hub
podcast.body: Located at 924 Gilman Street in West Berkeley, California, this venue is recognized as arguably the most important all-ages punk club globally. Founded in 1986, it operates as a member's only establishment, requiring a $2 annual fee for membership, which includes voting rights at bi-monthly meetings where club business is discussed. The club enforces strict rules: no drugs, alcohol, violence, racism, homophobia, or major label bands. Due to the major label ban, successful alumni such as Green Day, The Offspring, AFI, Primus, and Bad Religion are no longer welcome to perform there. "Probably the most important, all-ages punk club in the world."

podcast.title: Ambiguous Usage (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: By the mid-1970s, "punk rock" was used carelessly and liberally, with artists like Patti Smith, Aerosmith, Bruce Springsteen, The Rolling Stones, and even The Bay City Rollers being called "punks," indicating a lack of clear definition. podcast.body: While the Sex Pistols' aesthetic had a significant global impact, punk in America eventually developed its own distinct path in many aspects, even as it was initially influenced by the Sex Pistols' visual revolution. podcast.title: Antidote to Mainstream Rock (1970s)
podcast.body: Punk rock emerged in the 1970s as an "antidote" to the "preening and swaggering" of mainstream rock, offering a raw, unfiltered, and more authentic expression. "Punk became the antidote for the preening and swaggering of mainstream rock in the 1970s."

srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

podcast.title: Artistic and Social Revolution
podcast.body: Punk fundamentally altered perceptions of music, dismantling artistic, social, and demographic barriers, essentially leading a new generation of musicians to redefine rock and roll. "Punk changed the way people looked at music, breaking down artistic, social, and demographic barriers."

podcast.title: Association with Early Rock and Roll (1950s)
podcast.body: The release of "The Wild One" in 1953 coincided with the birth of rock and roll. The establishment soon conflated these two emerging forms of youthful rebellion, labeling young rock and rollers as "punks," meaning troublemakers, though this was still distinct from its later musical meaning. "So it wasn't long before the establishment managed to intertwine these two new forms of youthful rebellion. Young rock and rollers were also punks, but not in the modern sense."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Attitude Over Skill
podcast.body: Punk rock showed everyone that anyone who wanted to make music should be able to, asserting that only attitude mattered, rather than needing to be a professional musician with serious skills. This concept paved the way for a wide variety of music that would not have been possible before punk emerged. "Punk showed that only attitude mattered. podcast.title: Attitude as Foundation
podcast.body: According to Lester Bangs, the essence of performing rock and roll or punk rock boils down to having "nerve," asserting that it is fundamentally an attitude that, if possessed, allows one to engage with the genre regardless of external opinions. "Lester Bangs wrote, performing rock and roll or punk rock or call it any damn thing you please there's only one thing that you need nerve rock and roll is an attitude and if you got the attitude, you can do it no matter what anybody says."

podcast.title: Attitude of "Angry Young Men"
podcast.body: Elvis Costello, Joe Jackson, and Graham Parker adopted a "punk attitude" as they emerged from Pub Rock and Powerpop, which was instrumental in shaping the New Wave genre. podcast.body: The punk rock aesthetic prioritized attitude over musical ability, a characteristic that carried over into early Technopop. podcast.body: Mut Lang's early work with The Boomtown Rats injected a "crunch of punk" into their sound, combined with a punchy new wave sensibility, helping them score immediate UK hits. "The Irish band's singles with mutt had the crunch of punk but with a punchy new wave sensibility."

podcast.title: Bowie's Indirect Influence
podcast.body: David Bowie's "outsider-ness" in the early 1970s, his short, sharp songs, wild fashion sense, and defiant attitude appealed greatly to the working-class youth who would form the first generation of British punks. His friendships with figures like Iggy Pop and Lou Reed (of The Velvet Underground) also made him a "cool" figure for them, and his willingness to reinvent and "kill off" personas was highly admired. "Bowie's outsider-ness of the early 1970s endeared him to other people who felt alienated and marginalized."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's Indirect Influence
podcast.body: The audacity of David Bowie, particularly with his theatrical and fantastical approach to music and image as Ziggy Stardust, inspired British kids who were bored with the rock and roll mainstream. These individuals were later instrumental in starting punk rock. "Inspired by Bowie's audacity, later started something called punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's Influence and Distance
podcast.body: During the period of David Bowie's Berlin Trilogy, the punk movement was born and virtually died. Bowie maintained a cautious distance from punk but exerted a tremendous influence on it. "El es el abso de tiempo nació y prácticamente morió el punk, movimiento del cual mantuvo una prudente distancia pero al que influencian armemente."

podcast.title: Breaking Barriers for Mass Consumption
podcast.body: Punk successfully broke many barriers for the mass consumption audience, paving the way for the public to be more receptive to challenging movements like No Wave later on. "ya el pan cabía, digamos que roto muchas barreras para el público de gran consumo con lo cual a lo mejor el público ya estaba mucho más abierto a lo que era el movimiento no wave."

podcast.title: Breaking Gender Roles
podcast.body: Punk rock emerged in the 1970s and significantly disrupted many "inviolable gender roles" within rock music. Its core tenet was that everyone, including women, had the right to self-expression, regardless of who they were, leading to a reinvention of female musicianship. "Puncted many things for rock, including knocking down a lot of here-to-fore, inviolable gender roles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breaking Musical and Social Rules
podcast.body: Punk tore up established rules in the 70s, asserting that if one had something to say, they should say it, needing only "the guts to do it." This ethos was crucial in challenging conventional roles, such as women in rock music. "But punk tore up all those rules. Again, the primary premise of punk was, if you have something to say, say it, all you need is the guts to do it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Punk Ethos
podcast.body: British punk became a vehicle for rebellion, aiming to "kick against the upper classes and the monarchy," shock older generations, challenge established institutions, and destroy the status quo, effectively giving power to the powerless. "British punk went beyond just mere music. It involved kicking against the upper classes in the monarchy. It was about shocking the older generations. It was about challenging all manner of established institutions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Punk as Goth Origin
podcast.body: Gothrock originated as a spin-off from British punk music in the 1970s. "Gothrock began as a spin-off from the British punk of the 1970s"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Punk as Political Statement (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: By the end of 1975, punk in England was deeply rooted in political and class grievances. It was a reaction to a collapsing economy, widespread strikes, and a rigid class system that stifled opportunity. This intense movement aimed to shock older generations, challenge established British institutions, and destroy the status quo, thereby empowering the powerless. "In England though, punk had a different look and feel. While punk was more of an art statement in New York, it was fueled by politics in the class system in the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Punk as Total Rebellion
podcast.body: In mid-1970s Britain, punk music emerged as a comprehensive protest against the dire socio-economic conditions, including high unemployment, government austerity, and systemic class inequality. The music wasn't just against specific issues but expressed a profound rejection of the entire system, encapsulated as giving society, the government, and the economy "one big FU." No institution, not even the Queen, was spared from its critique. "The music wasn't so much a protest against something as it was a protest against everything. The whole idea of punk was to give society the government and the economy one big FU."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Satirical Comedy Show Reference (Early 1980s)
podcast.body: The satirical British punk comedy show "The Young Ones" featured a throwaway gag referencing David Bowie's "Ashes to Ashes," demonstrating the song's widespread cultural impact and recognition within the UK's alternative scene beyond just music charts. "the satirical British punk comedy show The Young Ones."

podcast.title: Built-In Drive Towards Self-Destruction – Symbolized by Sid Vicious
podcast.body: The original punk movement had an inherent drive towards self-destruction, which Sid Vicious came to symbolize. For some, this destructive impulse was seen as a poetic and artistic expression. "The original punk movement had a built-in drive towards self-destruction. Sid Vicious came to symbolize that."

podcast.title: California Punk as Predecessor
podcast.body: California punk rock is recognized as the main predecessor to American hardcore punk. "And so was punk rock, especially California punk rock, which was the main predecessor to American hardcore punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: California as a Center
podcast.body: A significant hub for punk rock activity during the 1990s was California, with major scenes flourishing in areas such as Orange County, the Bay Area, and the skate park suburbs of San Diego. "A lot of the big action seemed to be centered in California, Orange County, the Bay Area."

podcast.body: NoMeansNo is identified as a "fine Canadian punk band" from Victoria, active since the late 1970s, known for doing things their own way, which sometimes leads to trouble. "no means no, a fine Canadian punk band from Victoria who have been around since the late 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cassette Sound Influence (1980s)
podcast.body: The distinctive "cut" and "scratched" sound often associated with punk music, particularly prominent in the 1980s, was partly attributed to the inherent sound degradation of cassette tapes. This specific audio characteristic has been intentionally mimicked by contemporary bands like The Strokes in their recordings. "ese sonido cortado y ese sonido rasgado que tenía todo el punk y que tenía todo el roque de los 80 gracias a esas cintas de cassette."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Catalyst for British Explosion
podcast.body: The Ramones' July 1976 concerts in London are considered a direct catalyst for the "British punk rock explosion," as they taught "just about every single person who would become a major player" in the scene a transformative lesson. "just about every single person who would become a major player in the British punk rock explosion were taught a lesson by the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Catalyst for Synth Acceptance (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: The punk rock explosion played a significant role in the mainstream acceptance of synthesizer music, alongside the decreasing price and increasing portability of synth gear. It created an environment where unconventional musical approaches were embraced. "The second reason was the punk rock explosion."

podcast.title: Catalyst for Women in Music
podcast.body: Punk rock was profoundly important for women in music because its ethos prioritized expression and courage over traditional barriers like gender, age, or musical ability. This inclusive environment allowed many female artists to form bands and voice their perspectives without prior mastery of instruments. "One of the most important things to happen in women in music was punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Challenges of Aging in Punk
podcast.body: It is a common challenge for punk bands to sustain their career and identity as they age, as the genre's ethos often relies on a "young, loud, and snotty" persona. Maintaining this image later in life can make a band appear inauthentic. Green Day is cited as an exception to this typical downfall. "This has been the downfall of many a musician. It's like they all have this best before date stamped with their foreheads."

podcast.title: Challenging the Self-Destructive Stereotype
podcast.body: Greg Graffin of Bad Religion is presented as a prime example that a punk rocker does not necessarily have to be a "self-destructive moron," citing his extensive academic achievements and career. "If there's one guy who was shown that a punk rocker doesn't have to be a self-destructive moron, it's him."

podcast.title: Chinese Punk Scene
podcast.body: The punk genre is active in China, as evidenced by Seymour Stein's visit to the D22 club in Beijing where he listened to "band after band performed Chinese punk and alternative." Stein believed something significant was happening in China's music scene that would become "big everywhere." "Seymour found a stool near the front, closed his eyes, and listened to band after band performed Chinese punk and alternative."

podcast.body: Punk music and its subculture were central to the clientele and soundscape of Chocolate, especially during Tony Vitale's tenure. While sinister bands were prominent, Vitale also played "guitar-driven" bands like The Cramps and The Meteors, appealing directly to the punk and "ula siniestra" (sinister culture) communities. podcast.body: Over time in the United States, especially influenced by the scene at CBGB, the term "punk" became more specifically associated with bands like Ramones and their particular style. Bands that did not fit this narrower definition were then classified under New Wave. "se fue quedando el punk ya para la generación de los ramones y de la gente que hacía esas versiones, lo que conocemos en el punk."

podcast.title: Colonial American Usage
podcast.body: In Colonial America, a "punk" referred to a specific type of stick used for lighting fires, fuses, or fireworks. This usage was apparently appropriated from the Algonquin Indians of Delaware, who spelled it "P-O-N-K" and used it to mean dust, powder, and ashes. "In colonial America, it was a different story. A punk was a type of stick used to light a fire or maybe light a fuse or set off some fireworks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comeback (Mid-90s)
podcast.body: Punk music experienced a comeback in the early to mid-1990s, fueled by albums like Green Day's "Dookie" and The Offspring's "Smash." "Punk had made a comeback with albums like Green Days Duckey and the offspring Smash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Commercialization by Record Labels
podcast.body: In 1978, record labels like RCA were actively seeking out any group that resembled the Sex Pistols' punk sound or that played verbally aggressive music, seeing it as a lucrative opportunity for market expansion. "Ya durante 1978 pasaba que cualquiera que hiciste algo parecido por ver los instrumentos, un música verbalmente agresiva era objeto de dinero, entonces era como que tanto la RCA, pues como muchas otras discográficas estaban comentivamente a la caza de cualquier grupo que pudiesen echar un poco más mercado que diez, un poco ese aire pan de los expuestos."

podcast.title: Comparison to Folk Music
podcast.body: Dave Grohl likens punk rock to folk music, emphasizing its role in allowing young people to write about topics important to them, such as their neighborhood or home life, rather than generic rock themes. He suggests this makes it a form of "reporting" on real-life experiences. "it is like folk music in that you have these kids writing about things that are important to them. You're not going to have a kid in Springfield, Virginia, writing songs about Jack Daniels and mud wrestlers and limousines. You're going to be writing about what's going on in your neighborhood or your home and in that like folk music, it's kind of like reporting, you know, like you're writing about things that really happen to you."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Conspiracy Theory Origin
podcast.body: A government conspiracy theory posits that "punk" was a secret American nerve gas agent developed in the late 1960s. This weapon was believed to cause hair loss, except for a multicolored strip down the middle. Allegedly, victims of these clandestine experiments were shipped to England, where they wandered the streets of London, appearing drunk and vomiting. Some individuals, drawn by the unusual hair, began imitating them and, when questioned about their inspiration, responded "punk," thereby birthing the musical movement. "They say that punk was a government code name for a secret American nerve gas agent that was being developed in the late 1960s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Core Characteristics
podcast.body: Punk rock emerged as a reaction to the corporate influence on rock music, focusing on stripping down songs to their essentials. It typically features an urgent 4/4 beat, minimal to no drum or guitar solos, and generally simple lyrics. "The focus on punk was stripping down a song to the essentials And it has this urgent 4 or 4 beat, not a lot if any veering off into drum or guitar solos Um, lyrics were generally pretty simple."

podcast.title: Credo of Inclusivity
podcast.body: The 1990s began with Generation X's "restatement of the punk rock credo that anyone with anything to say should be allowed to say it regardless of musical ability, class, sex, religion, or race." This ethos denounced "isms of all kinds," especially sexism and racism, fostering an environment for genre blending. "the decade began with Generation X's restatement of the punk rock credo that anyone with anything to say should be allowed to say it regardless of musical ability, class, sex, religion, or race."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Critic's Scathing Assessment
podcast.body: One critic expressed an intensely negative opinion of punk rock, describing it as "nauseating, disgusting, degrading, ghastly, sleazy, pruriant, biogas, to congenially nauseating." This individual particularly singled out the Sex Pistols as "unbelievably nauseating" and "the antithesis of humankind," advocating that most punk groups "would be vastly improved by satan death" and that "the whole world will be vastly improved by their total and utter non-existence." "My personal view on punk rock is that it's nauseating, disgusting, degrading, ghastly, sleazy, pruriant, biogas, to congenially nauseating."

podcast.title: Cultural Movement
podcast.body: Punk is more than just a musical movement; it is a profound cultural movement that influenced many aspects of society. It manifested in literature, poetry, ideology, politics, artistic movements, and, most notably, a significant and enduring aesthetic. "El punk es un movimiento musical apasionante, entre otras cosas porque no es un movimiento musical, es como un movimiento cultural que lo influyó todo y que se reflojó muchas cosas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Cultural Storm Analogy
podcast.body: Punk rock's run from 1976 to 1982 was cited as an example of a "perfect cultural storm" in music, similar to the Beatles, grunge, and Britpop, lasting approximately six years. "Think of punk rock from 76 to 82."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: DIY Ethos
podcast.body: A core tenet of punk rock was the "doing it yourself" philosophy, which persisted even when the genre receded into the margins. This ethos ingrained itself into many subsequent genres, including post-punk. "And the central tenets of doing it yourself, engraved itself into many other genres loosely grouped under the umbrella of post punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: DIY Ethos
podcast.body: Punk rock championed the idea that it was no longer necessary to be an accomplished musician to make music, liberating and empowering new bands to form almost hourly. The "do it yourself" approach, demonstrated by bands like The Damned and Buzzcocks, encouraged groups to proactively record and release their own music cheaply through independent labels, making independent recordings prevalent by 1977. "Liberated and empowered by the fact that it was no longer necessary to be an accomplished musician in order to make music, new bands were formed almost hourly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: DIY Mentality and Evolution
podcast.body: During the 1960s and 70s, independent record labels played a crucial role in nurturing and promoting musicians who were exiled from the mainstream. This era, propelled by punk's do-it-yourself mentality, pushed for change and evolution from below. "On part one, we looked at the importance of independent record labels when it came to nurturing promoting musicians exiled from the mainstream during the 60s and 70s. This round pushed for change and evolution from below with their do-it-yourself mentality."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

podcast.title: Dancing and Anti-Fashion
podcast.body: In the 1970s, dancing was generally considered "uncool" by some rock fans, with the exception of pogoing or slam dancing performed at punk band shows. The punk scene also had an austere anti-fashion attitude, against which the New Romantics reacted with elaborate styles. "Dancing was seen as uncool, unless you were pogoing or slam dancing to a punk band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: David Bowie's Influence on British Punks
podcast.body: By 1975, David Bowie was a favorite among British punks, who appreciated his music, non-status quo fashion sense, and defiant attitude. His influence was so strong that most London punks at the time were also fans of Bowie. "By 1975, he'd become a favorite among British punks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Debunked KGB Creation Theory
podcast.body: A widely circulated but false story, originating from the satirical website World News Daily Report, claimed that the entire punk movement (including the Sex Pistols, The Clash, and Ramones) was a KGB plot. The fabricated narrative asserted that Soviet secret police financed punk to create chaos, pervert Western youth with nihilistic and anti-establishment ideologies, and even infiltrated mainstream radio to promote the music, describing it as one of the USSR's most successful propaganda experiments. "He claims that the entire punk movement from the sex pistols to the clash to the Ramones was financed by the Soviet secret police."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Defining Attitude (1970s)
podcast.body: The punk rock movement, particularly in the 1970s, was characterized by a "Free For All" attitude that empowered individuals to step on stage and express themselves. This environment was crucial for female musicians like Chrissie Hynde to demonstrate their guitar skills on par with men, despite the prevalent sexism of the era. "The Free For All, anyone with the guts to get up on stage and say something attitude of punk, gave her the opportunity to show that she could play a guitar just like one of the guys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Definition and Market Reward
podcast.body: Some artists were "punks before punk was a genre." While the "Angry Young Men" were not punks in the same vein as The Sex Pistols, they emerged during a period when playing "loud, fast and aggro" was rewarded by the marketplace. For Elvis Costello, his lyrical content was considered more punk than his musical style. "Some of these guys were punks before punk was a genre."

podcast.title: Definition as Attitude
podcast.body: Punk was understood less as a specific sound and more as an attitude. The core idea was that if one possessed something important to say and the courage to express it, they should do so, regardless of their proficiency as a musician or singer. "It's important to remember that punk wasn't so much a sound as it was an attitude."

podcast.body: Number 6 Denmark Street in London, an area known as the UK's "Tin Pan Alley," holds historical significance for punk rock as the location where the Sex Pistols first rehearsed, made their initial demos, and resided together. "number 6 Denmark Street was where the sex pistols first rehearsed and where they made their first demos. They also lived together on the upper floor. podcast.title: Desire to Shock Complacency
podcast.body: Fueled by a sense of hopelessness about their future and the future of their country, British punks aimed to shock people out of their complacency. "British punks felt hopeless about their future and the future of their country. They wanted to shock people out of their complacency."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Diffuse and Heterogeneous Nature
podcast.body: The punk movement is characterized by its diffuse and heterogeneous nature, with many distinct visions emerging from different cities and types of punk. This means there isn't a single, unified punk aesthetic or belief system. "El punk es un movimiento como muy difuso y muy heterogéneo, hubo como muchas ciudades, muchos tipos y muchas visiones del punk totalmente distintas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Disruption of Mid-1970s Rock Rules
podcast.body: Punk Rock emerged in the mid-1970s as a powerful reminder that musical rules did not always need to be followed, catalyzing a significant period of fragmentation, amorphousness, and mutation in music. "One of the great gifts of Punk Rock was a reminder that you didn't always have to follow the rules."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Disruptive Force in Music
podcast.body: Punk music is identified as having significantly "shaken" older music, leading to a greater openness among musicians to explore "new paths." This indicates its role as a powerful, transformative, and disruptive force in the musical landscape. "The older music had been shaken by punk so much that people were more willing than ever to find new paths."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Diverse Sounds Under the Label
podcast.body: The term "punk" in the 1970s encompassed a wide range of sounds, from the "pure punk" of The Ramones, to the "free verse" of Patty Smith, the "quirky funk rock" of Talking Heads, and the "genre hopping" Blondie. "From the pure punk of the remones to the free verse of Patty Smith, the quirky funk rock of talking heads to the genre hopping Blondie."

podcast.body: The 1990s witnessed the emergence and popularity of numerous punk rock subgenres, including pop punk, punk funk, hardcore, garage punk, glam punk, queercore, riot girl, and scop punk, showcasing its wide array of styles. "All different flavors too. There was pop punk, punk, punk, hardcore, garage punk, glam punk, queer core, riot girl, scop punk."

podcast.title: Do It Yourself Ethos (1970s)
podcast.body: A central tenet of punk rock was the "do it yourself" philosophy, encouraging musicians to create music regardless of their technical playing or singing abilities. The focus was on expressing a message by any means necessary and within any available budget, accepting amateurish sounds, imperfections, and mistakes like being out of key or out of time. "A central tenet of punk was, do it yourself. Don't worry if you can't play or sing. If you have something to say, then say it by whatever means necessary using whatever budget you have."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Documentation and Spread (Pre-Video Channels)
podcast.body: With no video channels available at the time, punk music was documented and disseminated through cool record stores, small publications (fanzines), and word of mouth, all originating from independent record labels and the artists they attracted. "So the only way the music got documented and spread was through cool record stores, small publications, and word of mouth."

srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Dogma and Escape
podcast.body: By the late 1970s and early 1980s, musicians were seeking freedom from the rigid dogma of punk, alongside an escape from disco, which encouraged experimentation in sound, visuals, and attitudes. "In new generation of musicians, we're freed from the rigid dogma of punk and an escape from disco..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Domino Effect on New Music
podcast.body: The punk scene created a "domino effect" that profoundly shaped the new music prevalent today, inspiring musicians like Elvis Costello, the founders of Joy Division, and The Clash to create their own music. "Here's one more story about how the punk scene set up a domino effect that helps explain the new music that we have today."

podcast.title: Dress Code
podcast.body: Punk fans typically adhere to a recognizable dress code, often characterized by jeans, t-shirts, and leather jackets, creating a uniform that signifies their tribal affiliation within the music subculture. "Punk's dress one way..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early 2010s Bleakness and Mid-Decade Revival
podcast.body: Punk faced a "bleak" period at the beginning of the 2010s due to the faltering of Pop Punk and Emo. However, by the mid-teens, things had improved, possibly influenced by political situations like Donald Trump's presidency and Brexit. This revival was categorized as Garage Punk and Post Punk, building on previous punk eras but showcasing a wide variety of approaches from artists like Against Me!, Sleater-Kinney, Japandroids, Fucked Up, Parquet Courts, Idles, and Sleaford Mods. "However, at the beginning of the decade, it did look kind of bleak." "If there's a way to categorize that mid-decade revival in Punk, it would perhaps be Garage Punk and Post Punk."
