podcast.title: Early 20th Century Criminal Connotation
podcast.body: In the early 20th century, Victorians began using "punk" to refer to a young criminal. Within the first three decades of the century, the connotation expanded to include the idea of being young and inexperienced, adding nuance to its definition. "By the early 20th century, Victorians were using punk to refer to a young criminal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Characteristics (1970s and early 1980s)
podcast.body: In its initial phase during the 1970s and early 1980s, punk was defined by its "loud, fast, angry and nihilistic" sound. This intense style gradually evolved into pop punk through the integration of more melodic and harmonic elements. "the loud, fast, angry and nihilistic punk of the 1970s and early 1980s morphed into the pop punk that is so big today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Conflict with Capitalism
podcast.body: When The Clash first emerged in 1976, they cultivated an image of "populist punk rebels with working class socialist politics," leading many to believe their stance was "completely incompatible with any kind of capitalism," including the record industry. "Many saw what the clash stood for as being completely incompatible with any kind of capitalism."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Definition vs. Later Representation
podcast.body: Debbie Harry noted that in its nascent stages, the punk scene was diverse, encompassing "a lot of different styles and a lot of different types of music." She observed that it was only later that the term "punk" narrowed to represent a particular kind of music, with genre labels often being applied based on the prevailing time period. "when it was happening, the punk scene embodied a lot of different styles and a lot of different types of music. It was only later that punk came to represent a particular kind of music."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 57 - Punk and New Wave at New York's CBGB

podcast.title: Early Definitions and Misunderstandings
podcast.body: The origins of punk are often debated, with its "official" birth typically attributed to New York and the United Kingdom between 1976 and 1977. However, the movement had precursors like Los Saicos (1964), The Sonics, and The Stooges, who played "savagely" before 1977. While these were early, miraculous, and brilliant efforts, a genre truly exists when there's a network of groups, an audience, a scene, media, venues, and a shared feeling that something new is happening, which was not the case for these early isolated acts. "Cada vez que hablo del pan que en algún vídeo llago referencia a su nacimiento durante los años 1976 y 1977 entre Nueva York y el Reino Unido, siempre aparece algún comentario que dice que estoy mal informado que estoy disinformando a la gente."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)

podcast.title: Early Era Ending (Early 1980s)
podcast.body: By the early 1980s, the original punk rock era had "birded itself out" but left behind a "spirit of adventure" that influenced the subsequent post-punk era and its experimental sounds.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Influence (1970s)
podcast.body: In her youth, Sinead O'Connor gravitated to early punk music, along with disco, Bowie, Bob Marley, and Barbara Streisand. This interest contributed to her non-conformist and rebellious artistic persona. "Later it was Bowie and Bob Marley and Disco in early punk, and Barbara Streisand."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Influence on Hugh Dillon
podcast.body: Hugh Dillon held Teenage Head, a punk band, in high regard, idolizing them and learning to play guitar from their album "Frantic City" and the solo from "Wild One." "I grew up idolizing Teenage Hits. One of the first records I bought, that was a rock record and I learned to play guitar from that first, from Frantic City."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

podcast.title: Early Influence on The Tragically Hip
podcast.body: Gord Downie's early exposure to punk rock included encountering "Rick and the Rodent S," a local punk outfit. Although he later grew tired of "punky covers" in The Filters, the energy and style of punk were part of his formative musical experiences. "Eventually he ran into another local band, a punk outfit called Rick and the Rodent S."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Major Label Rejection
podcast.body: When punk arrived in the 1970s, its radical nature meant most of the music was too extreme for larger labels, whose primary concern was maximizing record sales. Much punk and subsequent music was not mainstream enough for these major labels to invest in. "When punk arrived in the 1970s, most of the music was too radical for the bigger labels. Their main concern was to sell as many records as possible."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Music Simplicity
podcast.body: In the early days of punk rock, the emphasis was on raw energy and attitude rather than musical complexity, with the implication that even knowing "two notes" on an instrument was sufficient. "Okay, he knew how to play two notes, but hey, it was punk rock, right? You didn't need more than two notes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Origins in New York (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: Punk rock initially emerged in New York in the mid-1970s as an "artsy" movement. This early North American scene was generally less political and class-conscious compared to its later development in the UK. "Now punk began as an artsy sort of thing when it first emerged in New York in the middle 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Rock Conspiracy

podcast.title: Early Semantic Mystery
podcast.body: The term "punk" historically described a young male gangster or hood hundreds of years ago. Its first appearance in print in a music context as "punk rock" was in the Chicago Tribune on March 22, 1970, with Ed Sanders of The Fugs describing his solo album as "punk rock redneck sentimentality." "Now there's that word again. Punk? How did it end up being used to describe a certain type of rock music?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early US Phenomenon (New York City)
podcast.body: Before the Ramones' influential UK gigs in July 1976, punk rock in the US was largely confined to "scusier clubs in New York City," indicating its niche and underground status. "For the most part, this was a phenomenon restricted to some of the scusier clubs in New York City."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early US vs. UK Development
podcast.body: In the mid-1970s, punk rock was primarily a phenomenon restricted to "scusier clubs in New York City." However, with the Ramones' influential London gigs in July 1976, and the subsequent 100 Club Punk Rock Festival in September 1976, punk rock quickly "started to take off in the UK" and was no longer a secret. "For the most part, this was a phenomenon restricted to some of the Scusier clubs in New York City. Outside of a show, punk priestess Patty Smith had played a couple of months earlier, the Ramones appearance would be England's first proper exposure to US style punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Usage (1590s)
podcast.body: The word "punk" dates back to Old England around 1590, where it may have been used to describe a certain brand of male prostitute. This historical usage predates its musical application by centuries. "Old England about 1590. It may have been used back then to describe a certain brand of male prostitute."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Work for Willie Williams
podcast.body: Willie Williams, who later became a prominent tour designer for U2, began his career by doing lights for punk gigs in London, indicating the genre's role in his early professional development. "He got bit by the road bug early when he started doing lights for punk gigs in London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: We Are The Road Crew - A History of Roadies

podcast.title: Egalitarian Values
podcast.body: The emergence of punk rock introduced new egalitarian values into the music scene, fostering an environment where groups fronted, led, or even entirely composed of women were embraced by fans. "But punk brought in new egalitarian values, and fans embrace groups fronted by, led by, occasionally, consisting entirely of, women."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Egalitarianism and Opportunity for Women
podcast.body: Punk rock introduced an ethos of egalitarianism, asserting that anyone with something to express should be allowed to do so, irrespective of musical ability, class, race, religion, or gender. This movement was instrumental in opening musical doors for women during the 1970s more than any preceding era in musical history, thereby paving the way for numerous strong and powerful female musicians, despite persistent sexism. "The punk rock of the seventies opened musical doors for women more than any other era in musical history."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Elvis Costello's Unconventional Fit
podcast.body: Despite his folk singer and rhythm and blues background, Elvis Costello found himself categorized within the British punk scene, which was initially unexpected. His "sneer and anger and geekiness" helped him fit in, but his role as an angry singer-songwriter set him apart in an era where 99% of punk was coming from groups. "Although we came from a folk singer in rhythm and blues background, Elvis found himself lumped into the British punk scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Elvis Costello

podcast.title: Embrace of Inclusivity (1970s)
podcast.body: One of the defining characteristics of the original punk rock era in the 1970s was its radical concept that music should be accessible to everyone, and that anyone with something to say musically should be able to express it. This ethos actively dismissed traditional barriers such as age, background, class, ability, gender, and sexual orientation. "One of the great things about the original punk rock era of the 1970s was the concept that music belonged to everyone and that anyone should be able to make music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

podcast.title: Emergence in New York City
podcast.body: The concept of punk rock began to truly materialize at a small club located in one of the sleaziest parts of New York City, signifying a gritty, real-world origin for the genre. "And this is where we finally get to the concept of something called punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence in the UK
podcast.body: When the Ramones' debut album was released in April 1976, punk was nascent in the UK, described as "stirring" but not yet "coalesced into anything firm." The Ramones' performance at the Roundhouse in North London on July 4, 1976, is credited with doing "more to kick start British punk than anything else that had happened up until that point." "Punk was stirring, but it really hadn't coalesced into anything firm."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emo's Hardcore Punk Roots
podcast.body: Emo has its origins in the hardcore punk scene of Washington, D.C. However, it distinguished itself by focusing predominantly on emotional subject matter, such as breakups and angst, rather than the anti-authority rebellion typical of hardcore punk. "Its roots are in the hardcore punk scene of Washington, DC, but instead of rebelling against authority, emo is much more emotional."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emo's Pop-Punk Evolution (Late 1990s)
podcast.body: Towards the late 1990s, emo experienced a breakthrough, evolving to incorporate more poppy and punky elements. This shift included the integration of numerous hooks and melodies, making the genre more accessible. "It became more poppy as well as punky. Lots of hooks and melodies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emphasis on Expression
podcast.body: In its early stages, punk rock prioritized authentic self-expression and courage, making gender, age, or traditional musical ability secondary to the desire and guts to convey a message. "In the beginning, punk rock was all about having the guts to say something. That's what got you respect and attention. Gender, age, musical ability did matter. It was all in wanting to express yourself and having the courage to do it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emphasis on Freshness and Immediacy
podcast.body: Punk music, prior to Joy Division's emergence, was largely characterized by a focus on freshness, agility, and a preference for raw, first-take recordings. Joy Division's more reflective, deep, atmospheric, and absorbing approach to music was a radical departure from this prevalent style. "el pan que había dado como una visión muy fresca y muy muy ágil y muy muy de primeras tomas en la música y que alguien viniese como esa manera tan reflexiva y tan profunda, tan atmosférica, tan absorbente de trabajar la música era como muy innovadora."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: End of Original Form
podcast.body: By the summer of 1979, punk, in its initial mid-decade form, was considered "over," necessitating evolution for any remaining groups to survive. "By the summer of 1979, punk was over, in its original mid-decade form anyway. If the remaining groups wanted to survive, they needed to evolve."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Enduring Aesthetic
podcast.body: The punk aesthetic has persisted for decades, continuing to influence urban tribes, youth movements, and even re-inspiring fashion designers on catwalks today. "La estética punk, a un hoy en día, continúa para mucha gente, continúa para muchas tribus urbanas, continúa siendo la influencia de muchos movimientos estéticos en los jóvenes posteriores y, a un de vez en cuando aparece una pasarela de algún diseñador que ha decidido reinspirarse en el punk clásico."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Enduring Presence
podcast.body: Although punk rock experienced a perceived burnout at the end of the 1970s, it never truly died, continuing through bands like The Ramones (who kept touring) and Husker Du (who released records), as well as the establishment of American hardcore. "Now punk had always been around. Sure, it kinda got burned out at the end of the 70s, but it never died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Enduring Three-Chord Formula
podcast.body: Punk rock is characterized by its "tried and true three-core punk rock formula," a musical structure that has been in use since the late 1960s. While Green Day's sound wasn't innovative, they successfully kept this formula sounding fresh throughout their career. "Their sound isn't particularly innovative. They follow that tried and true three-core punk rock formula that's been around since the late 60s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Green Day: From their Beginning to 2005

podcast.title: Energetic Influence
podcast.body: The song "Crack My Spine Like A Whip" is described as having an "almost punky" energy, highlighting the genre's influence on the band's more high-octane tracks. "It just has a immediate energy to it, almost punky in a lot of ways."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Establishing a Logo "School"
podcast.body: Punk music established its own "school" of logo design, beginning with bands like the Ramones and their emblem based on the US Presidential Seal. "El Pum también creó escuela. Los primeros fueron los Ramones con su famoso logo."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Cómo los Logos Definieron la Música ｜ Símbolos de Resistencia

podcast.title: Ethos of Authenticity
podcast.body: The rise of grunge and alternative music in the early 1990s represented a return to the punk ethos of the 1970s, emphasizing authenticity, humbleness, and a lack of barriers between performers and audience. It championed music made by regular people for regular people. "Bottom line, basically returned to the punk ethos of the 1970s when there were no barriers between the performer and the audience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ethos of Expression Over Ability
podcast.body: In its formative years, punk rock valued the guts to express oneself above all else, including traditional musical ability, gender, or age. This emphasis on courageous self-expression allowed artists to gain respect and attention purely through their message and performance. "Gender, age, musical ability did matter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ethos of Freedom
podcast.body: The punk rock era of the 1970s fostered an ethos of "do whatever the hell you like," which unleashed music to fracture and evolve in many directions simultaneously. This freedom led to thrilling results and was a catalyst for the emergence of various alternative genres. "music, freed by the do whatever they held you like, ethos of punk, was able to ride off in all directions at once, with some very thrilling results."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ethos of Open Expression
podcast.body: At its fundamental core, the punk scene of the 1970s promoted the radical idea that anyone should be empowered to express themselves freely, regardless of their age, social class, gender, or perceived musical ability. While much of punk music was characterized by its loud, fast, and angry delivery, this foundational spirit of uninhibited expression ultimately also provided a philosophical basis for the emergence of gentler, more introspective forms of musical communication, such as prototweet. "At the heart of punk was the idea that anyone should be able to say what they wanted, regardless of age, class, gender, or musical ability."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution and Expansion
podcast.body: While early punk bands like the Ramones focused on "three chords really fast and screaming about how life sucked," The Clash significantly expanded the genre's musical scope by incorporating Ska, Reggae, Rockabilly, R&B, and even Rap into their sound. They also deepened punk's lyrical content to address alienation, working-class politics, racism, unemployment, and police brutality. This evolution ensured that punk did not "die out with a whimper by the beginning of the 1980s" but instead evolved into "a hundred different flavors," leading modern-day punk bands to owe a lot to The Clash.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution and Segmentation
podcast.body: By the close of 1977, punk was on the cusp of a significant evolutionary phase. This would lead to a vast array of new sounds that, while not strictly punk, unmistakably bore its influence, creating a "woozy, but in a good way" effect on listeners. "Punk was about to undergo a serious bit of evolution that would result in an array of sounds that was so big, it kind of made you woozy, but in a good way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution in the 1980s
podcast.body: By the early 1980s, even as legendary bands from CBGB had moved on, the club adapted to a "new generation of punks" who were described as "faster and angrier and messier," with bands like Murphy's Law and Bad Brains using the tiny stage as their proving ground. "There was this new generation of punks that arrived. They were faster and angrier and messier."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 57 - Punk and New Wave at New York's CBGB

podcast.title: Evolution into Hardcore
podcast.body: Far from dying out, punk rock evolved into Hardcore, primarily an American invention from the West Coast. This new form intensified the original punk formula, making it faster, more aggressive, harsher, angrier, and more violent, while also maintaining a strong anti-establishment stance. "And the most prevalent form was Hardcore, an American invention, mostly from the West Coast, that took the original punk rock formula, made it faster, more aggressive, more harsh, more angry, and more violent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Evolution of Sound
podcast.body: The mid-90s punk rock revival expanded beyond just "two and three chord songs played angry and fast," embracing diverse sounds and attitudes, including pop-punk and ska-punk, and reflecting a broader philosophical approach to music. "The mid-90s punk rock revival wasn't just about two and three chord songs played angry and fast. People started paying attention to groups like Blink 182, who were very punk in their attitude, but also quite pop in their songwriting."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution to Hardcore
podcast.body: Hardcore punk emerged as a subgenre from punk rock, specifically driven by creators who preferred the faster and heavier end of original punk bands and sought to express deeper grievances. "Hardcore punk, or just hardcore, if you prefer, is a subgenre, obviously, of punk rock. Its creators love the faster and heavier end of the original punk rock bands"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolutionary Leap
podcast.body: Hüsker Dü's *Zen Arcade* was described as a "huge evolutionary leap for punk" by combining the power and energy of hardcore with melody and more conventional song structures. "This was a huge evolutionary leap for punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Expansion and Crossover Attempts in the 1980s
podcast.body: At the start of the 1980s, several punk bands attempted to "stretch the definition of punk" and achieve pop chart hits, moving beyond its initial confines. "We're now at the start of the 1980s when several of these bands are trying to figure out how much they can stretch the definition of punk and score some actual pop chart hits."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: This Ain’t No Party! Edition Part 2

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: This Ain’t No Party! Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Exploding Scene in England
podcast.body: The albums Iggy Pop recorded with David Bowie were vital to the "exploding punk rock scene in England," significantly influencing the new, young, and extreme bands of that era. "Those albums that Iggy did with Bowie were important, not only to him, but to the exploding punk rock scene in England."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Explosion in Mid-1970s
podcast.body: Punk rock experienced an explosion in the mid-1970s, contributing significantly to the origins of alt rock. "If you're an alt rock fan, you've heard the story of how this all began with the garage band to the late 60s and the punk rock explosion of the mid 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: False Claims of Authorship
podcast.body: For many years, various figures, including the Sex Pistols, Malcolm McLaren, and Vivienne Westwood, claimed to be the originators of the punk aesthetic. However, these claims were later debunked, revealing they had copied or adapted earlier ideas. "Hemos ido desenmascarando a falsos padres de la estética punk durante muchos años, los expuestos reclamaron ser los padres estéticos del punk, el resultado que era mentira. Mal con Maclaren reclamó ser el verdadero artífice de la estética punk y el resultado que era mentira. Vivian Westwood, la diseñadora que yo creo que convirtió el punk como movimiento estético en las pasarelas. También resultó ser una impostora."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Fashion Influence of Jordan Mooney
podcast.body: Jordan Mooney, working at Malcolm McLaren and Vivian Westwood's Sex boutique in London, became a living advertisement for outlandish clothes (wild hair, daring makeup, see-through clothes, bondage gear). Her willingness to experiment with unconventional looks and her presence at Sex and with the Sex Pistols profoundly influenced the fashion sense of early British punk rock. "Jordan wasn't a singer, she didn't play any instruments but she did act as a magnet and then as glue for an important portion of the original British punk rock scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 2

podcast.title: First Generation Idols
podcast.body: The current era marks a period where the idols of the "first generation of punk rockers" are beginning to pass away, a demographic that once "thought they were going to live forever." "That first generation of punk rockers has now reached the age where their idols are starting to disappear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Modern Rock Scene on Indie Labels
podcast.body: Punk of the 1970s marked the first major music scene in the modern rock era built entirely on independent record companies. In Britain, punk rock's existence depended on independently-minded musicians and entrepreneurs because major, "respectable" companies and radio stations completely rejected it as "programming and ratings poison." "The punk of the 1970s was the first major music scene of the modern rock era to be built entirely on independent record companies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Formative Influence for Dave Grohl
podcast.body: For Dave Grohl, punk rock, specifically its authentic underground scene, was a profound and exciting discovery, contrasting sharply with the "ridiculous" portrayals he'd seen on television shows like *Chips* and *Quincy*. "Because the only punk I'd really ever seen was, you know, like on chips and Quincy and these TV shows that were just ridiculous. And it's all, often here it was, and I was so into it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Foundational Genre
podcast.body: Punk rock was a key part of Alexis on Fire's musical upbringing and evolution. The band considered their sound a natural progression from punk, through hardcore, and into post-hardcore and screamo, influencing their aggressive musical style. "We all kind of came up, I think, through Hardcore and punk rock and stuff like that. And this was just the next progression of that, you know?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Foundational Influence
podcast.body: Punk music, exemplified by bands like the Ramones, Sex Pistols, and Blondie, marked the beginning of a significant shift in the music scene, leading to the development of numerous subsequent genres and artists. "It started with bands like the Ramones and the Sex pistols and Blondie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Very First Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundational Values
podcast.body: The original punk rock explosion in the 1970s was centered on the idea of tearing things up and starting anew. It championed the belief that anyone should be able to express themselves, regardless of appearance, background, or gender, a novel concept at the time. "Now punk was all about ripping it up and starting again. If you had something to say, you should be able to say it regardless of who you were, what you looked like, what your background was, or your gender."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

podcast.title: Foundations of Modern Punk Rock – Drummers' Contributions
podcast.body: The foundations for modern punk rock were significantly influenced by figures who started as drummers, notably Iggy Pop and Joey Ramone. Iggy Pop's early career involved drumming for bands and Motown acts before he moved on to The Stooges and, through his later work, helped lay the groundwork for the genre. Joey Ramone, initially a drummer for The Ramones, contributed to songwriting from the drum kit before stepping out front to lead one of punk's most influential bands. "He started writing songs moved on to the stooges got involved with David Bowie took a lot of LSD and pretty much laid the foundations for modern punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fracturing into Hardcore (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: By the end of the 1970s, the original punk rock sound began to fracture and segment, with one of the most aggressive forms evolving into hardcore. This stylistic shift directly influenced the development of slam dancing and moshing. "But the end of the 1970s, the original punk rock sounds had fractured and segmented. One of those segments turned into hardcore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fusion in Southern Indie Rock
podcast.body: The "economy of punk" was a foundational element in the development of "jangly rock" in the Southern United States during the 1980s. This raw, efficient approach to songwriting and performance was fused with country rock influences to create an indie music sound that defined the decade and influenced bands like R.E.M. "jangly rock that fused the economy of punk with the country rock of Graham Parsons into an indie music that defined the 80s."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: A Little Love and Some Tenderness Edition Part 1

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: A Little Love and Some Tenderness Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Fusion with Reggae
podcast.body: As early as 1975, punk rockers began to flirt with reggae rhythms, exemplified by Patti Smith incorporating reggae elements onto her landmark album *Horses*. This connection was later made more overt by Elvis Costello and subsequently led to other bands like The Police adopting the approach. "As far back as 1975, when punk priestess Patty Smith threw a bit of reggae onto her landmark album Horses. Punk rockers had flirted with reggae rhythms."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Global Spread and Substyles
podcast.body: In the years following its emergence, the punk movement extended virtually worldwide, leading to the development of various substyles such as Oi!, Psychobilly, and Riot Grrrl. "Durante los siguientes años, este movimiento se extendió prácticamente por todo el mundo, derivando en varios opestilos, como el hoy, el Psycho Billy, o el Riot Girl."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Egg Punk: Explorando el lado más raro del punk

podcast.title: Godfather of Punk
podcast.body: Iggy Pop is widely regarded as the "godfather of punk" due to his pioneering stage antics, confrontational style, and the raw sound of The Stooges, which laid much of the groundwork for the punk rock genre. "And it's the beginnings of Iggy's legend as the godfather of punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Gothic Rock's Post-Punk Context

podcast.body: CBGB, originally envisioned for Country, Bluegrass, and Blues, became the "ground zero" for the emerging genre of punk in the mid-1970s. Following the collapse of the Mercer Art Center, avant-garde artists and early punk bands such as Television, The Ramones, and Patti Smith began migrating to the club, establishing it as the epicenter from which the genre's influence spread worldwide. "CBGB became ground zero for an emerging form of music called Punk."

podcast.body: During the punk era, Hammond B3 organs were often perceived as old, outdated, and associated with "dinosaur rockers." However, like other musical trends, its popularity eventually resurfaced. "There was a time during the punk era when Hammonds were seen as old, outdated, and part of the generation of dinosaur rockers."

podcast.title: Historical Influence
podcast.body: Punk rock emerged with an explosive impact in the 1970s and early 80s, playing a significant role in the broader development of alternative rock. Its influence, alongside grunge, continued to shape guitar-heavy sounds into the mid-2000s. "followed by the explosion of the 1970s and early 80s, the alt-rock nation days of the 1990s and the rise of Indy Rock in the first decade of the 21st century."

podcast.title: Impact on Concept Albums
podcast.body: When punk rock emerged with its characteristic two-minute, two-chord songs expressing "burning hate," it contributed to the concept album falling out of favor for a significant period. "When punk rock came along with its two-minute two-chord songs of burning hate, the concept album fell out of favor for a very long time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact on Female Drummers' Acceptance
podcast.body: The attitude fostered by the punk rock movement played a significant role in making the idea of a female drummer less of a novelty by the 1980s. Punk helped break down barriers and normalize women's presence in percussion. "By the time the 80s appeared, the idea of a female drummer was the novelty or foreign concept. The attitude of punk helped that a lot."

podcast.title: Impact on Music Industry
podcast.body: The punk revolution transformed the music industry, and its commercial success in the UK and USA prompted major record labels to sign riskier bands. This led to the formation of independent labels with non-commercial aims. "Tuvo que venir la revolución punk para poner la industria patas arriba."

podcast.title: Impact on Rock World (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: Punk emerged around 1977, simultaneously with disco, and "tore asunder the rock world," leading to fragmentation and the rejection of more challenging music by major multinational labels. "At the same time punk hit, tearing us under the rock world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact on Spanish Youth
podcast.body: Punk was the foreign cultural movement that had the strongest initial impact on young people in Spain following the end of the dictatorship. It characterized itself with raw energy and a desire to break with everything old. "El que pegó más fuerte a los jóvenes fue el punk."

podcast.title: Inclusivity and DIY Ethos
podcast.body: A lasting legacy of punk rock was the encouragement that anyone could make music, however they chose, fostering a do-it-yourself (DIY) aesthetic that allowed for diverse sounds beyond sounding like specific punk bands. "This idea that if you wanted to make music, then you should be able to make the music you want, however you choose to make it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence from David Bowie
podcast.body: David Bowie was a significant inspiration to the punk rock movement, contributing to its development by pushing rock into new areas of theater and spectacle and challenging conventional rock star imagery. "His inspiration to the punk rock movement, the new wave kids, the post-punks, including Tectopop, Electronic Agatha Industrial, his effect on the alternative generation from the Pixies to Nirvana to Nine-inch Nails to Arcade Fire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence of Nuggets Bands
podcast.body: Many of the artists featured on the "Nuggets" compilation became heroes and direct inspirations for the musicians who would go on to create the punk rock movement. "Many of these so-called Nuggets bands became heroes to the people who would soon create this new thing called punk rock."

podcast.title: Influence of The Clash
podcast.body: The "energy and the vision" of The Clash and the "risks they took" are credited with preventing punk rock from "fizzling out completely at the end of the 1970s." The band's contributions are fundamental for "three-cord, punk-inspired rock and everything that came after." "punk may have fizzled out completely at the end of the 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on "Roxanne"
podcast.body: The Police's signature song "Roxanne" is noted for its genre fusion, combining elements of reggae, punk, and rock. "It is not just the lyrics, of course. It's the arrangement in the mix of reggae, punk and rock."

podcast.title: Influence on Bass Players of the 1970s
podcast.body: The punk rock explosion of the 1970s was a significant period for influential bass players, characterized by a "just do it" attitude that encouraged musicians regardless of technical skill. "And now it's time to offer up some gratitude to the most influential bass players since the punk rock explosion of the 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Celtic Music
podcast.body: Punk rock, which took hold in Ireland in the 1970s (both the Republic and the North), had a profound impact on traditional Irish music. The boisterous, often dark and sad themes, and drinking songs inherent in traditional Irish music made the addition of a punk rock attitude a natural fit, leading to the development of Celtic punk. "Traditional Irish music can be boisterous, have dark and sad themes, and feature great drinking songs. And when you think about it, at a bit of punk rock attitude, really wasn't that much of a stretch."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Early Alt Rock (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: Punk music from the mid-1970s was a crucial component of the influences that eventually led to the Indie Rock Revival. It was part of a cycle that saw garage rock from the late 60s meet punk to form the basis of later alternative rock styles. "which itself was a repeat of the garage rock of the late 60s, made it with a punk in the mid 1970s."

podcast.title: Influence on Early Tattoo Culture
podcast.body: The Berlin underground punk rock scene, particularly as depicted in the movie "Christian F.," inspired Dave Grohl's very first attempt at a self-tattoo, showcasing punk rock's early influence on DIY body art. "I watched this movie that was a movie that took place in Berlin in the Underground punk rock scene. It was a movie called Christian F."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on New Rock
podcast.body: Punk rock and new wave from the 1970s are recognized as fundamental components that lend "extra credibility" to the sonic DNA of what is now defined as "New Rock." This highlights their enduring foundational role in the evolution of contemporary rock genres. "If some of this DNA can be traced back to the punk rock and the new wave of explosion of the 1970s, that's very good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Post-Punk and New Wave
podcast.body: Post-punk is a blanket term for new music made possible by punk, even if it didn't sound like punk. The new wave era (1978-1984) and its subgenres like Technopop were direct evolutionary outcomes of punk's attitude and its challenge to traditional musical norms, encouraging DIY and experimentation regardless of skill. "post-punk is the blanket term given to all the new music made possible by punk. It did not sound like punk, but it couldn't have happened unless punk did first."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Powerpop and New Wave
podcast.body: Although Powerpop itself wasn't punk, its integration with new wave heavily showed that "punk had definitely happened." Bands like The Buzzcocks, Elvis Costello, and Joe Jackson brought a "little punk into the mix," adding an aggressive edge to the melodic and hook-driven Powerpop sound. "It wasn't punk, but you could tell by listening to the New Wave brand of Powerpop that punk had definitely happened."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Riot Grrrl
podcast.body: Female pioneers of punk and post-punk, such as Patti Smith, Siouxsie Sioux, and Kim Gordon, provided direct inspiration for the Riot Grrrl movement in the early 1990s. "Taking inspiration from the female pioneers of punk and post-punk, it would be Patty Smith and Susie Sue and Kim Gordon of Sonic Youth, Chrissy Hine, Oni DeFranco, and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

podcast.title: Influence on Second Wave Ska
podcast.body: Punk music and its attitude played a significant role in the emergence of the second wave of Ska in the UK. Many early punks listened to Soul, R&B, Reggae, and Ska (Bluebeat) at clubs, leading to a mixing of these older sounds with the new punk scene. "And then a few years after that, the first British punks. Now back then, there were plenty of punk fans and a growing number of punk bands, but there were no punk recordings yet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Second Wave Ska
podcast.body: Working-class punk music from England was combined with traditional Jamaican Ska by white youth in Coventry in the late 1970s. This fusion gave the working-class music of Jamaica a new twist, contributing to the revival and new sound of Ska. "who gave this working class music from Jamaica a new twist by adding working class punk from England."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on The Go-Go's Origins
podcast.body: The Go-Go's emerged from the late 1970s Los Angeles punk scene, where they shared stages with other punk bands like X and The Germs, and incorporated punk's speed and attitude into their own sound. "The band came out of the late 1970s LA punk scene. They shared stages with groups like X in the germs."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Influence on Third Wave Ska
podcast.body: The American punk underground became enchanted with the British Ska revival (second wave) and consequently fused Ska with hardcore influences, contributing significantly to the rise of third-wave Ska in the early 1990s. "A segment of the American punk underground really became enchanted with the British SCAT revival. Given their background they inevitably fused SCAT with hardcore influences."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Lindsey Buckingham intentionally sought to address and incorporate the 1970s punk movement into Fleetwood Mac's music for the "Tusk" album, contributing to its experimental sound. "Dominated by songs from Lindsay Buckingham, who was intent on addressing the 70s punk and new wave movements within Fleetwood Mac's music..."

podcast.title: Influence on Weezer's Sound
podcast.body: Weezer's sound, particularly during their association with second wave emo, was noted to have a significant punk rock influence, distinguishing it from grunge. "And there was more than a little punk rock to their sound than Grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Initial Rejection for Mass Consumption
podcast.body: When record labels sought alt-rock beyond grunge, "pure punk was considered to be a little too strident, little too intense for mass consumption." Its unrefined nature was seen as unsuitable for widespread mainstream appeal. "At first, pure punk was considered to be a little too strident, little too intense for mass consumption."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Intensified Moral Outrage (1970s)
podcast.body: The emergence of punk music in the 1970s intensified the moral outrage among conservatives. Punk was specifically targeted for its "angry, nihilistic approach" and non-mainstream fashion styles, leading to accusations that it was transforming children into "rebellious, disrespectful, and anti-establishment goons" and calls for its suppression. "Then, the metal and punk of the 1970s just got them into more of a froth. This music is turning our children into rebellious, disrespectful, and anti-establishment goons. It must be stopped. Punk was singled out because of the music's often angry, nihilistic approach, not to mention the new fashion styles which were decidedly non-mainstream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Intertwined with Other Genres
podcast.body: By the end of the 1980s, punk, funk, rap, hip hop, and metal were "all becoming inextricably intertwined," setting the stage for new genres like nu metal. "So by the end of the 1980s, there were signs that punk, funk, rap, hip hop and metal were all becoming inextricably intertwined."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jack White's Early Exposure
podcast.body: Jack White (then Jack Gillis) was exposed to "all kinds of punk rock" by his upholstery shop mentor, Brian Moldun, at age 15, significantly expanding his musical horizons and influencing his later work. "While they were working, he exposed Jack to all kinds of punk rock, greatly expanding Jack's musical horizons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jacob Dylan's Preference
podcast.body: Despite his father being a famous folk singer, Jacob Dylan preferred punk bands like The Clash, The Buzzcocks, and The Jam in his youth. "he preferred punk bands like the clash and the buzz cocks as well as the jam."

podcast.body: Taylor Hawkins considered Jane's Addiction to be his "punk rock" because they presented a raw, authentic, and "disgusting" alternative to the "blah music" of hair metal that was prevalent at the time he discovered them. They resonated with him as a powerful and scary, yet awesome, new sound. "Same story. I mean, it's just that Jane's is your punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: John Frusciante's Early Love
podcast.body: Punk rock was John Frusciante's "first love" in music, exemplified by his admiration for the band The Jirms, which used "really weird punk rock tuning." "His first love was a punk rock band called The Jirms, simple stuff that used some really weird punk rock tuning."

podcast.body: While the KGB did not create the punk movement, they certainly viewed it as a potential tool to "screw with the West" and destabilize capitalist society, as evidenced by their attempts to court bands like Crass. Researchers found meticulous reports from KGB agents in Soviet-era Kiev concerned about youths enjoying punk music and examining its potential as a weapon against the West. "But did the KGB look at punk as a way of screwing with the West? Based on the story of crafts, the answer is, yeah, most certainly."

podcast.title: KGB Interest in Destabilizing Potential
podcast.body: The KGB, Stasi, and other Eastern Bloc secret police organizations were acutely aware of punk's potential to destabilize the UK and potentially all of Western Europe. They recognized its ability to tap into social unrest and anti-establishment sentiment, despite the movement not being a direct creation of Soviet intelligence. "There was no way that the KGB, the Stasi or any other secret police organization from the Eastern block were unaware of the potential for punk to destabilize the UK and perhaps all of Western Europe."

podcast.body: A theory, though largely debunked, suggests that punk rock was a KGB plot designed to destabilize the West. This theory posits that the Soviets sought to use punk's anti-establishment messages to create social upheaval, increase cynicism, promote revolutionary thinking, and encourage heavy drug use among Western youth, thereby bringing Western democracies into chaos. "Could it be that punk rock was actually a KGB plot against the West?"

podcast.title: KGB's Failed Attempts to Manipulate Western Punk
podcast.body: While the KGB did not create the punk movement, evidence from the Crass story suggests they "most certainly" attempted to exploit punk rock to foment hostility and destabilize the West. podcast.title: Kevin Lyman's "Punk Rock Summer Boot Camp"
podcast.body: Kevin Lyman, the founder of the Warped Tour, often referred to the grueling, low-paying, and tough environment of the tour as his "punk rock summer boot camp," suggesting that surviving the Warped Tour prepared bands for anything. "The Wonder Kevin Lyman often called Warped his punk rock summer boot camp."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kicking Against the Status Quo
podcast.body: British punk rock was fundamentally about rebelling against the established social order, expressing defiance towards the class system, the monarchy, and the perceived normality and humdrum lives of mainstream society. "British punk rock was all about kicking against the status quo, down with the class system, down with the monarchy, down with all you normal people in your humdrum lives."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lack of KGB Success
podcast.body: Despite the KGB's interest in potentially using punk to foment hostility in the West, there is no evidence to suggest they achieved any real success in destabilizing Western societies through such means. The claim that the KGB created punk is explicitly dismissed as false. "But did they have any real success by doing so? The answer seems to be no, at least as far as we can tell."

podcast.title: Late 1970s Decline
podcast.body: By 1978, punk rock was widely considered to be "dying," having "burned itself out after just a couple of years." Despite its rapid decline in its initial form, its legacy endured, fostering a freeform attitude towards music seen as essential for the advancement of rock and roll. "Punk Rock was dying. It had burned itself out after just a couple of years, but its legacy was still valid."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Late 70s/Early 80s Scene
podcast.body: The punk scene of the late 1970s and early 1980s was a fertile ground for bands like the Talking Heads, who emerged with rhythmically complex sounds that pushed post-punk musicianship. "Out of all the bands to emerge from the punk and new wave scene of the late 70s in the early 1980s, the talking heads were easily the most rhythmically complex."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Legacy of British Punk
podcast.body: The profound impact of British punk was so intense that its elements from the 1970s scene are still discernible and felt in contemporary punk music and culture. "The effect of punk was so intense that we still see and feel elements of that scene from the 70s in today's punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Legacy of DIY Ethos
podcast.body: Although many original punk bands of the 1970s were short-lived, the movement left a crucial legacy: the belief that "enthusiasm and access should be the only prerequisites for making rock and roll." It championed the idea that anyone could make music, regardless of age, sex, race, economic background, or even musical ability. "Infusiasm and access should be the only prerequisites for making rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Legs McNeill's "Punk" Fanzine (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: Legs McNeill, a fan of Manhattan's underground scene, founded a fanzine he eventually renamed "Punk." This decision was inspired by the cover art of The Dictators' "Go Girl Crazy" album, which depicted the band in leather jackets, leading McNeill to conclude they looked like "punks." The fanzine's growing circulation helped popularize the term for New York artists around CBGBs. "So that became the name of his fan scene. Punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Les Paul Guitar's Versatility
podcast.body: The Gibson Les Paul guitar has been continuously in production since its 1952 introduction and is widely used across virtually every genre, including punk. Its solid-body design resolved feedback issues common with older hollow-body guitars, making it ideal for amplified punk music. "The Les Paul has been in production ever since, and has been used by guitars into rock, punk, metal, pop, country, soul, R&B, jazz, reggae, and virtually every other genre you want to mention."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Liberating Philosophy for Women
podcast.body: The core philosophy of early punk rock, emphasizing self-expression regardless of musical ability or identity, proved incredibly liberating for many young women. This ethos fostered an environment where female drummers like Paloma Romero (Palmolive) could emerge rapidly. "One of the central tenants of the original punk rock scene was that if you had something to say, you should be able to say it, no matter who you were or what kind of musical ability you might have or not have."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: History of Female Drummers

podcast.title: Liberation of Gender Roles
podcast.body: Emerging in the 1970s, punk rock played a crucial role in dismantling previously rigid gender roles within rock and roll, which had traditionally confined women to pretty singing and shaking a tambourine. Its core principle was the universal right to self-expression, regardless of gender, which empowered women to redefine themselves as musicians in diverse and unconventional ways, leading to a flourishing of unique female performers. "Punk did many things for rock, including knocking down a lot of here-to-fore, invi-o-ble gender roles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Limitations and Evolution
podcast.body: While initially impactful, punk's limitations, such as its often angry themes and reliance on two or three chords, led to cross-pollination with pop music, eventually birthing New Wave. "As cool as punk was, it did have its limitations. I mean, how long could you go on being so angry, thrashing over two or three chords?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Limiting Nature
podcast.body: After an initial period of revolutionary excitement, some young musicians began to distance themselves from punk, perceiving its emphasis on anger and fast, three-chord thrashing as "limiting." It was seen as "so 1976," suggesting a growing desire for musical evolution beyond its rigid dogmas. "I mean how long could you go on being angry and thrashing three chords really fast? I mean punk was so 1976."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Listeners Have Longest Average Workouts
podcast.body: According to a study by Test Fitness Equipment, individuals who listen to punk music while exercising tend to have the longest average workouts, lasting approximately 53 minutes. "for those who listen to punk while working out, tend to have the longest average workouts at fifty three minutes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: London's Punk Years
podcast.body: The late 1970s, specifically 1976 and 1977, were known as the punk years in London, characterized by a collapsing economy, widespread strikes, high unemployment, rolling blackouts, and entrenched class system issues. This environment directly influenced bands like The Clash. "Inspiration was taken from what they saw around them in London during the punk years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Longevity of the Scene
podcast.body: The original punk rock explosion of the mid-1970s "came and went in about three years," demonstrating that a scene does not need to be long-lived to have a lasting impact. Its brief but intense existence left a permanent mark on music history. "Think about the original punk rock explosion of the middle 70s. It came and went in about three years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Los Angeles Adoption
podcast.body: Los Angeles, a natural home for the alienated and unconventional, quickly adopted punk rock once records from New York bands like the Ramones and singles from the Sex Pistols began circulating. The scene was driven by themes of alienation, hopelessness, and a desire to challenge the status quo. "LA had always been a place for the alienated the outcast and the weird, so it was a natural place for punk to land."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lyrical Evolution (Late 1970s - Early 1980s)
podcast.body: While early punk, exemplified by bands like The Ramones, contributed to a period of "shameful" lyrics in the late 1970s, it later saw a significant lyrical evolution. Ian Curtis, with Joy Division, took punk lyrics into an unknown sphere, exploring psychological, intimate, and personal suffering, transforming its expressive capabilities. "Sobre todo, yo creo que el final de los 70 es como una época bastante vergonzosa para las letras, tenemos desde la música disco, que hablamos muchas veces, pero también tenemos el inicio del PAN, va a refiró los Ramones, sus letras."

podcast.title: Mainstream Historical Origin
podcast.body: Most music historians trace the deepest roots of punk back to the late 1950s and early 1960s. Figures such as Iggy Pop are credited with helping to set the stage in the late 1960s and early 1970s for the genre's major explosion in the mid-1970s. The term "punk" itself is said to have originated from various sources, including a New York fanzine dedicated to this emerging music. "Most music historians, including me, well, have you give you a long, rambling account of how punk's deepest roots can be found in the late 50s and early 1960s?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mainstreaming of "Alternative" and "College Rock"
podcast.body: By the late 1980s, the music business began mainstreaming "alternative and college rock music" that the CBGB bands had helped to spawn in the 70s. This culminated in the launch of Billboard's Modern Rock chart in September 1988, which finally caught up to the sounds originating from the punk scene. "Speaking of rock radio, the music business had begun mainstreaming the so-called alternative and college rock music that the CBGB bands had helped to spawn back in the 70s."

podcast.title: Major Labels' Co-optation and Ignorance
podcast.body: Major record labels eventually "picked off the most commercially acceptable bits" of punk, rebranding it as New Wave and marketing it extensively. Anything deemed unusable or too radical was "essentially ignored," contributing to the development of a distinct underground scene. "Instead the major record labels picked off the most commercially acceptable bits called it New Wave and proceeded to bleed a dry."

podcast.title: Major Labels' Indifference (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: When punk rock first appeared in the mid-1970s, major record labels in North America showed no interest. They were preoccupied with the significant profits from established rock bands like Led Zeppelin, Pink Floyd, Fleetwood Mac, and The Eagles, as well as the booming disco scene. "In punk rock first appeared in the middle 1970s, the major record labels in North America did not care."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Malleability
podcast.body: Punk rock is noted for its high malleability, allowing it to take on many forms and serve multiple purposes for different people globally. "One of the things I love about punk rock is that it's very, very malleable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Market for Adolescent, Sophomore, Goofy Pop Punk
podcast.body: There existed a "stupidly huge market for adolescent, Sophomore, Goofy, Pop, Punk," which played a significant role in the massive global sales of albums like Blink-182's "Enema of the State." "On the other hand, there was a stupidly huge market for adolescent, Sophomore, Goofy, Pop, Punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Memphis Rap Affinity
podcast.body: The homemade and rule-breaking nature of early Memphis rap, both in its forms and production, made it closer to punk than to the polished records of major East and West Coast studios. This spirit informed its raw aesthetic. "Más cercano al pan que en formas y en producción que ha discos grabados en los grandes estudios de Los Angeles a Nueva York."

podcast.title: Mid-1970s Dogma
podcast.body: The original punk rock of the mid-1970s was instrumental in challenging gender prejudices in music, promoting the idea that anyone with something to say should be able to express it, regardless of musical ability, social class, race, or sex. This ethos allowed many women to enter the scene and was a foundational inspiration for Riot Grrrl. "The original punk rock of the mid-1970s was a great help thanks to the movement's dogma that anyone with anything to say should be able to say it, regardless of musical ability, social class, race, or sex."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mid-1970s Emergence
podcast.body: Punk rock rose in the middle of the 1970s, initially seen as an "aberration," a niche for "weirdos and misfits and outliers," and dismissed as "just noise" by rock purists who thought it would fade away. However, it persisted and is still discussed today. "There's one other event that we need to include on this list, and that's the rise of punk rock in the middle of the 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mid-60s Garage Rock Visuals
podcast.body: Throughout the 1960s, a series of rough, ragged, and raw-sounding garage bands from North America (including The Seeds, Count Five, The Barbarians, The Standells, and The Troggs) adopted a tough image, often wearing leather jackets. This look, reminiscent of Marlon Brando or James Dean, led some observers to describe these musicians as appearing like "punks." "And so it was inevitable that some people said the jackets made these guys look like punks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mid-90s Massive Renaissance
podcast.body: After being a niche genre for years, punk rock experienced a "massive renaissance" starting in the spring of 1994, coinciding with Kurt Cobain's death, which created a void that punk was able to fill. "But then an interesting set of circumstances came into play that resulted in a massive resurrection, an interest in punk rock. And echoes of that resurrection are still being felt today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mid-90s Revival
podcast.body: The mid-90s saw a "punk rock revival," signifying a resurgence of the genre's energy and attitude within the alternative music scene of the decade. "The mid-90s punk rock revival."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Midnight Screenings as Punk Rock Culture
podcast.body: The phenomenon of *The Rocky Horror Picture Show* midnight screenings, where audiences dressed up, yelled at characters, danced to the music, and created routines, was described as "very punk rock." This grassroots, interactive fan culture kept the movie and its soundtrack alive after its initial commercial failure. "It was all very punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Minimalist Music Requirements
podcast.body: In the early 1980s punk rock scene, the musical requirements for bass playing were minimal, with the statement "you didn't need more than two notes" reflecting the genre's raw and simple aesthetic. "Okay, he knew how to play two notes, but hey, it was punk rock, right? You didn't need more than two notes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Moby's Foray with Animal Rights
podcast.body: Moby ventured into the punk scene with his album *Animal Rights*, abandoning his electronic sound in an attempt to advance his career, at a time when guitar-based music was strong in the US. "con el animal rights se adentraba en la escena del punk."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Mohawk - Definitive Punk Rock Hairstyle
podcast.body: The Mohawk haircut is recognized as the quintessential and defining hairstyle of the punk rock movement, evolving into numerous variations over several decades. "Now the Mohawk remains the definitive punk rock hairstyle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Big Bang Analogy
podcast.body: Punk rock in the mid-1970s is likened to a "musical big bang" because the ideas and attitudes it generated spread out in all directions, eventually coalescing into new ideas and attitudes, forming entirely new musical "life forms" while sharing basic elements. "If we look at the punk rock of the middle 1970s, we can think of this as a musical big bang. The ideas and the attitudes it generated spread out in all directions and eventually began to coalesce into new ideas and attitudes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Maturation and Evolution
podcast.body: As original punks aged and their values shifted, many amateur musicians who entered music through punk became more proficient at their instruments. The simple, snarling lyrics over two or three chords became insufficient, prompting music to evolve beyond its initial form. "Everyone from the punk days was a few years older. These and values had changed. Some of the amateur musicians who got into music because of punk were now pretty good at their instruments. Snarling lyrics over two or three chords just didn't cut it anymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: NYC Birthplace
podcast.body: America considers CBGB in New York City to be the birthplace of its punk scene. "On today's episode we will examine the former biker bar in New York that America considers to be the birthplace of its punk scene, CB GB."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 57 - Punk and New Wave at New York's CBGB

podcast.title: Negative Connotations in the UK
podcast.body: In the United Kingdom, the term "punk" was initially not widely used due to its strong negative connotations, including violence and anti-establishment sentiments, and its association with anarcho-political movements. This led to "New Wave" being used for non-punk underground music in the UK. "en el reino nido la palabra punk no se usaba mucho porque tenía connotaciones muy negativas, ni aconotaciones violentas, ciertas con otaciones antisistema, porque venía a dar un poco del reino nido donde el punk estaba asociado, incluso a ciertos movimientos políticos anarquistas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: New Romantics' Rejection
podcast.body: The Blitz kids, who later spurred the New Romantic movement, became bored with the "angry nihilism of punk." They sought a more glamorous and fun aesthetic as a counterpoint to punk's starkness. "The Blitz kids, as they were called, had grown bored with the angry nihilism of punk and wanted something more fun and glamorous."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New York Dolls' Catalytic Role
podcast.body: The New York Dolls were crucial to the punk rock scene, to the extent that "without them, we might never have seen that spark that caused that incredibly important punk rock explosion in New York in the mid-1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: New York Origins
podcast.body: Punk initially began in New York City as a "low-key, artsy sort of thing," cultivated by alienated artists in economically depressed areas like the Bowery, who gravitated to venues like CBGB. "To recap, punk started in New York as a low-key artsy sort of thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New York Punk as Art Statement (Early 1970s)
podcast.body: In the early 1970s, New York punk emerged against a backdrop of urban decay, functioning primarily as an art statement. It was anti-materialistic and nihilistic, fostering experimental and non-commercial music in venues like CBGB, attracting a diverse group of artists, poets, writers, and fashion designers. "New York punk was, beyond all else, an art statement. It was anti-materialistic. The attitude was nihilistic. The world is coming to an end, so we may as well have a good time thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New York Scene - Johnny Thunders
podcast.body: Johnny Thunders was a key figure among the original New York punk rockers of the 1970s. "Johnny was one of the original New York punk rockers of the 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New York Scene in 1970s vs. 1990s
podcast.body: In the mid-1970s, the original punk scene in New York City produced a "ton of bands." However, by the late 1990s, the New York rock scene was considered "dead," with hip-hop flourishing but few rock acts emerging and limited venues for them to play. "Back of the old days, a ton of bands were coming out of the original punk scene. The late 90s? Well, not so much."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New York Scene – Early Hubs and Small Community
podcast.body: The original punk scene in New York was a tightly-knit community consisting of only a few dozen "weirdos." They frequented iconic venues located in the city's "uglier end," such as CBGB, the Mud Club, and Maxx's Kansas City, which became central to the scene's development. "The original punk scene in New York consisted of a few dozen weirdos who hung out at places like CBGB, the Mud Club, and Maxx's Kansas City, in the uglier end of town."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New York Times Description
podcast.body: A music critic for the New York Times described the Ramones as "a highly stylized extension of the punk idiom," noting their "non-stop set of brisk, monochromatically intense songs, where conventional considerations of pace and variety are thrown calculatedly to the wind." "The Ramones are a highly stylized extension of the punk idiom."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New York vs. British Punk (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: The punk rock explosion of the mid-1970s saw distinct ideological differences between its origins. In New York, punk was primarily for "artsy outsiders," with major bands like the Ramones, Blondie, and Talking Heads not being overtly political. Conversely, punk in Britain was intensely political, arising from a context of high unemployment, government financial struggles, industrial decline, widespread strikes, entrenched class systems, and general hopelessness, leading to music that protested "against everything" including the Queen. "In New York, where it all started, punk was for artsy outsiders... But on the other side of the Atlantic, punk was all politics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nirvana's Founding Influence
podcast.body: Kurt Cobain and Chris Novoselic bonded over punk rock in high school, particularly hardcore punk, which was a foundational influence for their first band, The Stiff Woody's. "Richard and Chris met up in high school and bonded over punk rock, especially hardcore punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: No Longer a Secret (Post-100 Club Festival)
podcast.body: After Britain's first official punk rock festival at The 100 Club in September 1976, punk rock ceased to be a secret. This event propelled the genre into wider public awareness, leading to its rapid escalation in popularity. "After the punk rock festival of September 1976, punk rock was no longer a secret and things just kind of went crazy after that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nomenclature Development
podcast.body: The term "punk" for the musical genre began to solidify in the mid-1970s in New York. The emergence of fanzines like "Punk Magazine," founded in 1975, played a crucial role in building the language, aesthetic, and attitude of punk, helping to consolidate the term within the burgeoning scene. "Desde ese momento, el término empezó a consolidarse."

podcast.title: North American Reception (1970s)
podcast.body: Punk did not gain traction in North America as it did in the UK. It was seen as too political, class-oriented, crass, vulgar, and violent, leading to radio stations refusing to play bands like The Ramones and record labels fearing to release records by The Clash in America. Critics also dismissed it as a fad. "One could never really cut on in North America, the same way that it did in the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

podcast.title: North American vs. British Evolution
podcast.body: While in North America, post-punk sounds were marketed as "new wave" (a less angry, violent, and political cousin), the British punk scene burned intensely for less than three years, with a growing backlash against original punks by mid-1979 as safety pins and swastikas in fashion became quaint or offensive. "However, things were different on the other side of the Atlantic. The original British punk seemed burned very bright and very loud for less than three years. And by the middle of 1979, the sex pistols had broken up and there was a growing backlash against the other original punks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Numerous Subgenres
podcast.body: Punk rock encompasses a vast array of subgenres, which are compared to the numerous ways one can prepare shrimp. These varieties include hardcore punk, sky punk, cyber punk, synth punk, anarco punk, cow punk, gypsy punk, Christian punk, Celtic punk, art punk, garage punk, glam punk, crust punk, horror punk, street punk, melodic punk, afro punk, skate punk, chicano punk, folk punk, and troll punk, among others. "Punk rock comes in as many different varieties as shrimp does."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Old School Revival
podcast.body: Leading up to the mid-1990s, there was a growing revival of interest in "old school punk rock," referring to the punk that predated hardcore, from bands like the Ramones, The Clash, and the Sex Pistols, which was hard and fast but also had a singable quality. "It just so happens that there was a building revival in the interest for old school punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: One-Hit Wonders
podcast.body: One-hit wonders appeared across the Punk genre in the 1970s, which made sense given the open nature of the music industry and Billboard charts at the time. "We saw them in Glamrock, Disco, Soft Rock, Punk, which makes sense because this was still the time when the music industry and the Billboard charts were wide open."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Origin and Definition
podcast.body: The most famous manager of the punk rock era, Malcolm McLaren, was frequently called a "Sphin Gali" for his manipulative tendencies. Bernie Rhodes, another prominent manager of the original British punk rock era, claimed to have invented punk rock by recruiting Johnny Rotten for the Sex Pistols.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin as Garage Rock Revival
podcast.body: Punk Rock, emerging in the mid-1970s, is identified as the first formal revival of Garage Rock. The term "punk" itself had even been previously used to describe some original 1960s Garage Rock bands. This new form maintained the basic DNA of Garage Rock but was generally louder, angrier, faster, and sometimes more politically charged. "The popularity of the Nuggets collection, combined with the rise of Iggy Pop and the studious and a few other like-minded bands, prompted the first garage rock revival, except now that it was being called punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Origin of Alternative Music
podcast.body: The entire concept of alternative music was born out of the punk rock explosion of the mid-1970s. Its angry guitars directly led to a variety of post-punk sounds. "Now, the whole concept of alternative music was born out of the punk rock explosion of the middle 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin of Goth Music
podcast.body: Goth music emerged as a direct byproduct of the British punk rock explosion of the late 1970s. "Goth music cleaves off from the original British punk rock explosion from the late 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin of Pogo (1970s UK)
podcast.body: The Pogo dance became prominent during the original punk rock era in the UK in the 1970s. In many venues lacking stages, bands played on the floor at audience level. To see the band, attendees would jump up, leading to the Pogo's development. "The Pogo became a thing during the original punk rock days in the UK back in the 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Original Antagonism Towards Pop
podcast.body: Punk music was initially conceived and developed as an "attack on pop," establishing an inherent opposition to mainstream popular music and its conventions. "Punk was originally created as an attack on pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Original Characteristics
podcast.body: Early punk bands were typically characterized by their fast, loud performances and often expressed highly political and socially aware themes. They commonly professed a disdain for the preceding generation of bands, although some, like The Sex Pistols and The Ramones, subtly or overtly demonstrated popular music influences. "The original punks were fast and loud and often very political and socially aware. And they professed to hate much about the previous generation of bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Original Mission and Context (1970s)
podcast.body: Born between 1974 and 1976, punk rock was conceived as the adversary and destroyer of the prevalent pop music on AM Top 40 radio. It emerged from challenging urban environments like New York and London, marked by high youth unemployment, with a clear mission "to obliterate that schmultzy, wimpy, sand metal crap" that dominated the airwaves. "When punk was born in the 1970s, it was designed to be the enemy, the destroyer of pop music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Original Wave
podcast.body: Bands like Talking Heads emerged from the original wave of punk in the 1970s. Their connection to this foundational movement allowed them to be among the first bands featured on MTV when it launched, showing the evolution from punk to new wave and beyond. "Bands like Talking Heads, who came up in the original wave of punk, were one of the first bands played on MTV."
