Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Origins in New York
podcast.body: Punk rock first emerged in New York in the mid-1970s, initially characterized as an "artsy sort of thing." While early progenitors like the MC5 were notably political, the North American punk scene was generally less political or class-conscious compared to its UK counterpart. "Now punk began as an artsy sort of thing when it first emerged in New York in the middle 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins in Tiny Clubs
podcast.body: Punk rock emerged from "tiny scary clubs" on both sides of the Atlantic, indicating its grassroots, underground origins far removed from mainstream music venues and industry attention. "So why would they bother with this weird stuff bubbling up from tiny scary clubs on both sides of the Atlantic?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins of New Wave
podcast.body: New Wave emerged as punk rockers raged in the mid-to-late 1970s. Musicians were drawn to punk's free expression but not its anger, aggression, violence, and politics. New Wave music could not have existed without punk, indicating an inextricable relationship. "This was music that wasn't punk, but could not have happened unless punk had gotten their first."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

podcast.title: Pacific Northwest Christian Punk Scene
podcast.body: The Pacific Northwest, particularly Seattle, cultivated a scene of "punky and grungy indie bands" with religious affiliations in the early 1990s. These bands struggled to get signed by mainstream labels due to their religious themes and were considered "too heavy" for traditional Christian record companies, leading to the formation of Tooth and Nail Records. "When he noticed that there were a number of very good, punky and grungy indie bands in the Pacific Northwest that couldn't get signed to a mainstream label because of their religious connotations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Palatability of Pop Punk
podcast.body: The emergence of pop punk made the genre "more palatable" for audiences who found the raw, "pure punk" sound "a little too intense." This adaptation broadened punk's appeal to a wider audience. "more palatable for those for whom pure punk was a little too intense."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Paving the Way (Late 1970s-Early 1980s)
podcast.body: Along with New Wave, punk "helped us through disco and paved the way for the music video generation." "Punk and New Wave helped us through disco and paved the way for the music video generation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Peak and Legacy of the Mid-90s Revival
podcast.body: The punk rock revival of the 1990s largely peaked between 1994 and 1996, though major acts like Green Day, The Offspring, and Blink 182 continued their success. This period led to the emergence of numerous punk bands, many of which are still active, and laid the groundwork for future groups like Simple Plan, Fall Out Boy, and My Chemical Romance, with its impact still felt today. "The punk rock revival of the 90s peaked through 1994 to 1996 before a rand of gas with the exceptions of a few bands. Green Day, offspring, Blink 1-2. But in their way came a long, long list of punk bands, many of which are still with us today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Peak of the Genre
podcast.body: The release of the Ramones' third album, *Rocket to Russia*, on November 4, 1977, occurred just as punk rock was peaking, cementing the album's importance. "Rocket to Russia was out just as punk rock peaked."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Perceived as "Bad for Business" by Rolling Stone
podcast.body: Following the poor reception of their Sex Pistols cover, Rolling Stone writers were reportedly instructed to stop covering punk music, with the sentiment that "punk's bad for business." This reinforced the mainstream's dismissal of the genre. "After that, most Rolling Stone writers were instructed to stop writing about this music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Perennial Nature and Generational Rediscovery
podcast.body: Punk is described as a genre that "never goes away," embodying an attitude and aesthetic that has persisted for nearly 50 years. Every generation since the 1970s has rediscovered punk and adopted its "fierce do-it-yourself ethic," which has been strengthened by technology's role in democratizing music. "Now Punk never goes away." "That attitude and aesthetic has been with us for nearly 50 years, and it cannot be killed and it will not die."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

podcast.title: Pez Name Dispute
podcast.body: An American punk band named "Pes" on BIO Records challenged Pezz's name in 1996, indicating the presence of other bands in the genre using similar names. "It was another punk band named Pes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Pilgrimage to Iggy Pop
podcast.body: Seeing Iggy Pop perform during his collaboration with David Bowie was considered "almost akin to making a pilgrimage to some holy ancient punk shrine" for many young, hungry extreme bands in England, highlighting his iconic status and influence. "Going to see Iggy during that Peru was almost akin to making a pilgrimage to some holy ancient punk shrine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Pioneering in the USSR
podcast.body: Punk music in the USSR was considered extremely radical, even too extreme for controlled venues like the Leningrad Rock Club. Anti-Panov (Zbind) is credited as the first punk of the USSR, marking the genre's early, audacious presence. "Pero hay algunos grupos que eran demasiado extremos para un club vigilado por el KGB. Uno de ellos fue este que no me atrevo a pronunciar. Su líder, Antraipanov, conocido como Zbind, es considerado el primer punk de la URSS."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Viktor Tsoi. El padre del Postpunk Ruso

podcast.title: Pogo Dance Origin
podcast.body: The Pogo, a dance involving jumping up and down in place, originated with British punks. It likely developed because early punk shows often lacked stages, requiring audience members to jump to see over others. As the music became more aggressive, Pogoing evolved into slam dancing. "Basically it involved jumping up and down in place. And probably started because so many early punk shows didn't have a stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Resurgence in 1990s
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, following the explosion of grunge music, the traditional boundaries between mainstream rock and the alternative music scene dissolved, creating an environment ripe for a new generation to discover and embrace various forms of punk rock. "Punk had always been there, waiting to be discovered by a whole new generation. And finally, in the 90s, the time was right."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Post-Refurbishment Use of Rolling Stones Mobile Studio
podcast.body: Following its refurbishment, the Rolling Stones Mobile Recording Studio became a favored tool for recording live performances by numerous punk bands, starting with the Ramones. "The truck was used to record live performances by a long line of punk bands from the Ramones on down."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pre-Punk Influence
podcast.body: The Stooges are widely recognized as a foundational "pre-punk" band, with their 1969 debut album going down in history as one of the most important pre-punk records of all time. Their raw and primitive sound significantly predated and influenced the punk movement. "It has gone down on history as being one of the most important pre-punk records of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Precedent for Radical Identity
podcast.body: Punk in England is highlighted as a historical example of a genre that successfully converted music into a radical identity, a cultural achievement that Gabber later replicated within the electronic music sphere in the Netherlands. "lo que el punk en Inglaterra vuelve la meta en Noruega, convertir la música en una identidad rarical."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Qué fue el GABBER y por qué asustaba a Europa

podcast.title: Precursor to Post-Punk
podcast.body: Punk rock is identified as the foundational genre without which post-punk could not have existed. Post-punk bands were not punk rock themselves, but their sound was clearly a descendant, indicating that punk had "happened" first. "In the case of post punk, for example, the term is used to describe a band or sound, which isn't punk rock, but listening to them, you could tell that punk had happened."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Predominant Aesthetic Image
podcast.body: The most widely recognized punk aesthetic, largely popularized by the Sex Pistols in the early 1980s and exported globally, includes plaids, Dr. Martens boots, chains, leather, and ripped clothing. "La gran imagen que tuvieron los expuestos, que hicieron como famos a la estética punk y que acabó predominando a primeros de los 80, como la estética de los expuestos, acabó siendo como exportada todo el mundo. Cuando pensamos en el punk, pensamos en los cuadros, pensamos en las Martins, pensamos en las cadenas, pensamos en el cuero, pensamos en todo esa cosa estética bondada, pensamos en la ropa rota."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Preference for Flexi-Discs
podcast.body: Many punk bands show a notable affinity for flexi-discs, frequently utilizing this format for special releases. "a lot of punk bands love them too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prioritizing Freshness Over Technicality
podcast.body: Punk music prioritized fresh, immediate, and newly created sound over technical correctness. This approach mirrored Black Sabbath's early disregard for polished production in favor of raw energy and directness. "primaba mucho la música fresca y la música recién salida sobre la técnicamente correcta."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Progress for Women in Music
podcast.body: The emergence of punk rock and artists like Joan Jett, Pat Benatar, and Lita Ford at the start of the 1980s, followed by Melissa Etheridge, Annie Lennox, and Madonna by the end of the decade, reflected significant "progress, not perfection," in women achieving their rightful place in music. "Brass and pocket and the other music that was on the verge of being made by Joan Jet, Pat Benatar, lead afford as the 80s began. And then Melissa Etheridge and Annie Lennox and Madonna by the time the 80s ends all reflect progress, not perfection, but progress in women taking their rightful place in music."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Protest Fashion and Doc Martens
podcast.body: Punks adopted Doc Martens as a form of "protest fashion" because these boots were seen as unpretentious, working-class footwear, providing a stark contrast to the Birkenstocks favored by hippies. Their practical steel toe was also useful in confrontations, fitting perfectly with the punk uniform of jeans, jackets, and mohawks. "Punk's and skinheads adopt the shoe as a protest fashion thing. These were unpretentious working-class boots, the exact opposite of the Birken stops worn by hippies. And they went perfectly with a punk uniform of jeans instead of jackets and mohawks. The steel toe was also handy in a fight."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Proto-Grunge Flavor – Slower, Sludgier, Deeper Style
podcast.body: A specific "proto-grunge" style of punk rock emerged, characterized by a slower, sludgier, and deeper sound. Many bands contributing to this genre recorded their material with Jack Endino at Reciprocal Recording, and this style was prominently featured on the *Deep Six* compilation. "It was called Deep Six, and it featured bands into this slower, sludger, deeper flavor of punk rock, many of whom recorded their contributions with Jack and Reciprocal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Provoked Genesis
podcast.body: Punk rock did not emerge spontaneously but rather was provoked into existence in the mid-1970s. Key figures and cultural shifts laid the groundwork for this revolution, reacting against the perceived over-sophistication of mainstream rock. "Now, this thing did not materialize out of nowhere. It had to be provoked into existence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Public Misunderstanding in North America
podcast.body: The general public in North America largely failed to understand or embrace punk rock. This was evidenced by the poor sales of Rolling Stone's fall 1977 issue featuring the Sex Pistols, which was one of the magazine's worst-selling covers ever. "The general public in North America just didn't get punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Public Nausea and Calls for Death (1970s)
podcast.body: In the 1970s, punk rock was met with extreme public disgust, described as "nauseating, disgusting, degrading, ghastly, sleazy, pruriant, biogas, to congenially nauseating." There were even calls for the musicians to meet "sudden death" and for their "total and utter non-existence." "My personal view on punk rock is that it's nauseating, disgusting, degrading, ghastly, sleazy, pruriant, biogas, to congenially nauseating."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Punk Band's Anti-Taping Statement (Dead Kennedys)
podcast.body: The punk band The Dead Kennedys, exemplified a unique form of protest against home taping. Their cassette version of the "In God We Trust, Inc." EP featured a blank B-side with an explicit message addressing the perceived threat of home taping to record industry profits. "when the punk band, the Dead Kennedys released the cassette version of their In God we trust Inc. EP. They left the B side blank with this note. Home taping is killing record industry profits. We left this side blank so you can help."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Digital Debris Part 1: B-Sides and Bonus Tracks

podcast.title: Radio Blackout (USA)
podcast.body: In 1978, mainstream rock radio stations in the United States refused to play punk rock, labeling it as "too dangerous, too weird, too violent, too polarizing, too class conscious, too political." The American industry generally regarded punk as a temporary fad that should be ignored until it naturally faded away. "Mainstream radio stations wouldn't touch punk rock. Too dangerous, too weird, too violent, too polarizing, too class conscious, too political."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Radio Hostility
podcast.body: In the late 1970s, American mainstream radio stations vehemently rejected punk rock, viewing it as too dangerous, weird, violent, polarizing, class-conscious, and political, often refusing to play any music associated with the term. "They hated anything associated with that word. There would have oaks music that was too dangerous, too weird, too violent, too polarizing, too class conscious, and too political."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Ramones' Enduring Influence
podcast.body: The "Ramon style punk rock" is noted for being reinvented numerous times, exemplifying the concept of "Standing on the Shoulders of Giants" where artists build upon previous achievements to advance music. "And how many times has Ramon style punk rock been reinvented? It's called Standing on the Shoulders of Giants, building on the accomplishments of those who came before us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ramones' Foundational Influence
podcast.body: The Ramones are widely credited as the band that did the most to kickstart punk rock, laying down the fundamental blueprint for the genre. "The death of Joey Ramon, the beginning of the end of the original lineup of the Ramones, the band who did more to kickstart punk rock than any other."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

podcast.title: Ray Davies' Definition of True Punks
podcast.body: Ray Davies of The Kinks approved of "true punks" like the Ramones or Lou Reed, contrasting them with bands he felt were merely "jumping onto" the punk trend, similar to how some bands adopted R&B earlier. He believed genuine punk offered an opportunity to convey ideas and opinions, a principle he applied in songs like "Father Christmas." "Instead he approves now of true punks, like the Ramones or Loom Reed, but not the bands jumping onto it the way bands got onto the R&B kick."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Reaction Against Over-Elaborate Rock
podcast.body: Punk emerged as a crucial reaction against the over-elaborate and complex philosophies of psychedelic and progressive rock, aiming to return to the more youthful, fun, and less complex origins of rock. "el pack tiene un importantísimo componente de reacción a esa filosofía de lo que era la música psicodélica y el roxico delico."

srcs.episode: Qué es el NO WAVE. Es mucho más que música

podcast.title: Reaction to Overproduction
podcast.body: Punk rock emerged as a reaction against and rejection of the "overproduction of some 70s rock," favoring a stripped-down, aggressive sound. "Harrison said that the band appreciates punk rock's rejection of and reaction to the overproduction of some 70s rock."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 57 - Punk and New Wave at New York's CBGB

podcast.title: Reactionary Force
podcast.body: Punk rock emerged in the 1970s as a potent reactionary force against the prevailing rock scene, aiming to strip everything back to basics and start anew. "Meanwhile, punk comes along as a potent reactionary force where everything is ripped up and everybody starts again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reactionary Nature
podcast.body: Like Ska, the Alt Rock version of punk was not revolutionary but reactionary, often serving as a response to the status quo in mainstream music. "Like punk, the Alt Rock version of SCA wasn't revolutionary. It was reactionary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reactionary Nature
podcast.body: Like grunge, punk was a reactionary movement, implying a shared philosophy of stripping back artifice in rock music. "Like punk, Grunge was reactionary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reading Festival Adoption
podcast.body: The Reading festival became the first major festival to embrace British punk music, alongside British new wave and British metal. "It also became the first major festival to really embrace British punk and British new wave as well as British metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rebellion Through Domesticity
podcast.body: Jazz Domino Holly, daughter of punk rocker Joe Strummer, rebelled against her "rock and roll childhood" by embracing traditional female pastimes like knitting, seeing it as the "other way" to go. Her mother was a punk and her grandmother a hippie, so she learned knitting from her great-grandmother, aspiring to reclaim traditionally female pastimes. "Because I had such a rock and roll childhood, the only way for me to rebel was to go the other way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Recording in Old Church Halls
podcast.body: Many punk and post-punk bands found a suitable recording environment in Wessex Studios, an old church hall in North London known for its live sound, creating a notable contrast between the genre's raw energy and the historic setting. "I think it's got a while that all these punk bands recorded in an old church hall."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Redefinition by The Clash
podcast.body: Joe Strummer, as a key member of The Clash, was instrumental in redefining punk rock, moving it beyond its initial "three chords and an attitude roots" to encompass broader musical and political themes.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Rejection by Post-Punk
podcast.body: *Metal Box* by Public Image Ltd symbolized a profound break from the punk scene, rejecting its limits and dogmas to forge new musical paths. "Metalbox suponía el nacimiento de algo nuevo, algo que nunca java en las reglas del punk, que rechazaba sus límites y sus dogmas"

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: Rejection of Norms
podcast.body: Punk rock, by its inherent nature, was a "rejection of the expected of the ordinary," which naturally led its bands to create politically and sexually charged songs that challenged societal conventions. "By its very nature, punk rock was a rejection of the expected of the ordinary, so the fact that punk rock bands would lead the way in writing songs that were politically and sexually charged is no surprise."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Rejection of Progressive Rock
podcast.body: The punk and New Wave movements actively sought to counteract the "lugubrious, intricate, wady" characteristics that were highly valued by fans of progressive rock. "These were what the musicians I'm going to focus on today were trying to counteract."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Relationship to Bubblegum
podcast.body: Tom Verlaine of the punk band Television provocatively suggested that punk music never truly existed, but was merely a "more aggressive form of Bubblegum," a statement that enraged John Lydon of the Sex Pistols. "Tom Verlaine of the punk band television said years later that punk music never really existed and that it was just a more aggressive form of Bubblegum."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: Resurgence in Early 1990s
podcast.body: The early 1990s saw a "resurgence" in punk rock, indicating a renewed interest and output in the genre during that period. "there was also a resurgence in punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Revitalization of a Christmas Classic
podcast.body: Darlene Love's 1963 classic "Christmas (Baby Please Come Home)" was given a "punk rock after life" by Joey Ramone approximately 20 years before 2020. "which was first given a punk rock after life by Joey Ramone about 20 years ago."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Revival in the Mid-2010s
podcast.body: Straight-ahead punk music experienced a revival in fashion around the mid-2010s, indicating a renewed interest in its sound and aesthetic. "About a decade later, there was another revival. Straight ahead, punk came back into fashion as did emo, shoegays, and various flavors of psychedelic music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: Right to Self-Expression
podcast.body: A central principle of punk rock was the belief that any individual had the right to express themselves in any manner they wished. This inclusivity was particularly liberating for women, freeing them from traditional expectations in music and allowing for diverse forms of self-reinvention. "The central tenet of punk was that anyone should have the right to say anything and any matter they wished, regardless of who they were."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rise in Early 90s
podcast.body: Alternative rock was on the rise in the early 90s, with bands like Nirvana topping the charts, influencing the music landscape around the time of the 1992 Grammys, though the Academy chose to go "fully pre-rock" that year. "alternative rock was on the rise and R&M and Nirvana were topping the charts".

podcast.title: Rise of Independent Labels
podcast.body: People who appreciated the radical new punk music started independent labels to provide an outlet for it, as mainstream labels showed no interest. These independent labels became known as "alternative labels," and the music they promoted was "alternative music." "But there were people who appreciated this radical new music and started new independent labels because they loved it so much and wanted to give it an outlet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Role in Concept Album Decline
podcast.body: Punk, alongside Alt Rock, played a significant role in the disappearance of the concept album in the 1980s and 1990s, viewing such projects as "vestiges of old rock" that needed to be "expunged from the culture." "Punk and Alt Rock had a lot to do with its death because these types of projects were seen as vestiges of old rock and needed to be expunged from the culture."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Roots in Black Sabbath's Early Sound
podcast.body: The punk movement is directly linked to the early albums of Black Sabbath, particularly their raw, fresh, spontaneous, and technically unpolished sound. This emphasis on immediate and unrefined music, along with a free approach to social provocation, became a core influence for punk. "el panque se basa yo creo que sin duda en los primeros discos de Black Sabbath es el referente no tanto a lo mejor en la temática pero sí en la manera de provocar a la sociedad."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Black Sabbath: Y así nació el HEAVY METAL

podcast.title: Safety Pin Aesthetic
podcast.body: The punk fashion aesthetic was significantly influenced by New York punk Richard Hell, who famously held his decomposing clothes together with safety pins. Malcolm McLaren, inspired by this look, and Vivienne Westwood, his partner, subsequently introduced this distinct style in their clothing shop, shaping the early visual identity of punk. "Malcolm McLaren had been inspired by how a New York punk named Richard Hell held his decomposing clothes together with safety pins. So he took that idea back to his partner Vivian Westwood, who introduced that look in their shop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: San Francisco Eclecticism
podcast.body: San Francisco punk was arguably the "most eclectic" of all the early punk scenes, uniquely blending elements of the artsy, the angry, and the city's established hippie, drug culture, and left-wing political traditions, which paved the way for later rock, new wave, and technopop sounds. "It often combined the best of the artsy side of things with the best of the angry side. And of course, there was the hippie side with its drug culture and left-wing politics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Separation from New Wave
podcast.body: In the late 1970s, Malcolm McLaren, manager of the Sex Pistols, played a key role in actively separating "punk" from the broader "New Wave" movement, advocating for the specific use of the term "punk" for his associated artists. "El fondo de las primeras personas que machaco mucho en instalar la versión punk, la versión de la palabra punk para todo este movimiento."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Seven-Inch Singles Collection Niche
podcast.body: Specializing in collecting seven-inch singles from punk bands is identified as a specific and popular niche within the broader hobby of record collecting. "Maybe you'll specialize in seven inch singles from punk bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shared Aesthetic with Synth Pop (1970s-1980s)
podcast.body: Bands like OMD saw a "punk sensibility" in playing synths. Just as punk guitarists might thrash one chord, electronic musicians could create new sounds with limited traditional musical ability. This embrace of new tools and rejection of rock clichés was considered a "punk thing to do." "One thing that a lot of people also don't realize is that there was a certain amount of punk rock aesthetic when it came to, by bands like you, who, you had no musical ability, at least not, while you were, you were, we were self taught."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Shared Stages with Pezz
podcast.body: Pezz frequently shared stages with other punk rock bands like Flashlight Brown in the early Toronto music scene. "back in the day, like we would play with, you know, flashlight brown and there were like a punk rock on a scob band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Shift in Message
podcast.body: Punk's central message of "screw you" was re-evaluated by a new generation of groups witnessing the British Empire's decline. They concluded the punk message was backward, reflecting a sentiment of "we're screwed" instead, feeling that punks, like hippies before them, had failed to achieve their aims. "If punk's central message was screw you, these new groups had a different outlook. They looked at the British Empire crumbling around them and decided that the punk message was wrong. They got it backwards. It wasn't screw you. It was... We're screwed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shift to Darker Music
podcast.body: As the original punk scene faded, individuals with a darker sensibility began to coalesce around existing dark music, leading to the formation of the Goth scene. "As the original punk scene died away, the darker minded slowly coalesced around those who already made dark music at least part time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Short Hair as a Tribal Identifier
podcast.body: In the mid-1970s, punk rock brought back short haircuts, largely as a rebellion against the long hair associated with hippies. Punks viewed hippies as having failed with their peace and love message, so short hair became a key identifier for the punk rock tribe. "So short hair became a way of identifying with the tribe of punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Simplicity and Accessibility
podcast.body: Punk rock is characterized by its simplicity, often utilizing just three chords, making it highly accessible for aspiring musicians who may be intimidated by virtuoso rock stars. This ease of entry allowed kids to start bands and write songs about their immediate surroundings and concerns. "And then you hear a Ramones song and it's three chords and you can do that and then you have friends that might not play drums like Buddy Rich or but they can play drums like the guy from the Sex Bistels or because it's so simple, it becomes available to you like, oh cool, well, I could start a band if we do it like this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Skateboarding Culture Bond
podcast.body: By the late 1970s, skate culture began to bond strongly with punk rock, a connection that made sense given their shared ethos of speed, risk-taking, aggression, working through anger, anti-establishment sentiment, and raw adrenaline. "But by the time we got to the late 1970s, skate culture had begun to bond with this new thing called punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Social Significance (1970s Britain)
podcast.body: Punk rock in Britain emerged from a deeply troubled society in the mid-1970s, characterized by the Arab oil embargo, an endless recession, widespread strikes, high youth unemployment, and a rigid class system. It provided a genuine social outlet, a "blow-up" for the frustration, anger, and energy of a generation that felt there was "no future." "There is a genuine social point to punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Soulful Infusion in The Gaslight Anthem
podcast.body: The music of Brian Fallon and The Gaslight Anthem is distinctly infused with a soulful sort of punk rock, a characteristic that defines their sound. "While the music of Brian and the Gaslight Anthem is definitely infused with a sulfal sort of punk rock, they're also singing about yearning and dreams from someone caught on the big city or someone who lives in the heartland in hopes to make it to the big city."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Stagnation and Evolution to Post-punk
podcast.body: Despite its initial impact, punk began to stagnate, becoming enslaved by its own rules which ultimately limited its creativity. This stagnation led to the emergence of post-punk, which expanded punk's disruptive attitude with experimentation. "El punk caracterizado con su energía cruda y sus ganas de romper con todo se había vuelto a esclabo de sus normas las cuales acabaron limitando su creatividad."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La España Siniestra ｜ La edad de oro del Postpunk y el Dark wave

podcast.title: Straight Edge Movement
podcast.body: A branch of punk rock known as Straight Edge advocates for abstaining from all drugs and alcohol. "This year a member of the branch of punk called Straight Edge, which issues all drugs or alcohol, or a member of the more ascetic teetooling branch of the Christian rock scene, alcohol is pretty much everywhere in rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Streetsville Music Scene
podcast.body: Mississauga's Streetsville neighborhood had a notable punk rock music scene, where Anthony Carone grew up and played guitar in punk rock bands during his younger years. "I grew up in Mississauga in Streetsville, nice little punk rock music scene there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Stripping Rock to Basics
podcast.body: Punk was not revolutionary but reactionary, simplifying rock music back to its fundamental foundations, thereby freeing the next generation of musicians to rebuild using different tools and attitudes. "Punk itself was not revolutionary. It was reactionary. It stripped rock back to its very basics, the foundations of rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Stylistic Transformations
podcast.body: Punk is mentioned as a genre from which artists like Bobby have drastically evolved, moving to instrumental music before returning to punk. This illustrates the potential for extreme stylistic jumps within an artist's career, sometimes becoming part of their core identity. "Bobby, ha pasado de hacer punk, hacer música casi en mental para después volver a hacer punk."

podcast.title: Successor to Bubblegum Music
podcast.body: By the close of the 1970s, punk music emerged as a dominant force, taking over from Bubblegum Music. This shift marked a significant change in popular music trends, as punk passed the torch from its predecessor. "By the end of the 70s, Bubblegum Music had passed the torch on to punk."

podcast.title: Sum 41's Live Performance Style
podcast.body: Sum 41's live performances are characterized as "very punk rock," featuring a big, loud, brash, and in-your-face energy, with frontman Derek Whibley often appearing "like a man possessed." "very punk rock."

srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Survival in Margins
podcast.body: Despite being overshadowed by synthesizer bands, hair metal, and pop music in the 1980s, punk rock music and its attitude never truly died. It mutated into sub-genres like hardcore, oi, and anarcho punk, surviving in local enclaves across North America, supported by dedicated communities. "It's not like punk was dead, but it had receded into the margins, drowned up by the waves of synthesizer bands, hair-middle groups, and various floods of pop music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Synonymous with New Wave in US (Initially)
podcast.body: For many years, particularly in the United States, "New Wave" was almost synonymous with "punk." This is evidenced by Sire Records' 1977 compilation titled "New Wave" that included bands like Ramones, who were pure punk. "en Estados Unidos todavía eran reacios, y se seguía usando el new wave casi como sinónimo de punk durante muchos años."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Taylor Hawkins' Hidden Listening
podcast.body: Due to the prevailing reggae scene in Orange County, Taylor Hawkins had to "hide" his Rush and Queen records from his brother and his friends. These bands became his personal "punk rock" because they were rebellious choices against the local norm. "So my punk rock became Rush and Queen and stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Technological Accessibility
podcast.body: Towards the very end of the 1970s, synthesizer technology became sufficiently affordable for young musicians involved in the original punk rock scene to incorporate these machines into their music-making, signaling a shift towards electronic sounds. "And at the very end of that decade, the technology had become cheap enough for young musicians in the last months of the original punk rock scene to adopt these music-making machines as their own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The 1970s Explosion
podcast.body: The original punk rock explosion of the 1970s served as a "major reset for rock and roll," described as a "great musical decluttering" where music was stripped back to basics. It embodied a reactionary spirit against the perceived lack of revolution in the 70s, emphasizing a DIY attitude that led to what would become alternative music. "The original punk rock explosion of the 1970s was two things. First, it was a major reset for rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: The Cramps' Counter-Narrative
podcast.body: While often associated with the punk movement, The Cramps publicly stated they did not identify with it. They argued that punk "disavowed the origins of rock and roll and wanted to destroy everything," whereas The Cramps embraced and celebrated rock's historical roots as "mythomaniacs." "Ellos decían no sentirse identificados con el movimiento, ya que el punk renego a los orígenes del rock and roll y quería acabar con todo, en cambio de Crams eran unos mitómanos."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Amor, Terror y Psychobilly: La Historia de The Cramps

podcast.title: The Stooges as Blueprint
podcast.body: The three studio albums and famous bootleg "Metallic KO" by The Stooges became crucial blueprints for the punk movement that emerged in the 1970s and 80s, inspiring future bands with their raw and violent approach. "Those three studio albums and that famous bootleg became blueprints for the punk that was to follow in the 1970s and 80s."

podcast.title: The Stooges as Template
podcast.body: The first three albums by Iggy Pop and The Stooges became some of the most crucial templates for what would eventually be known as punk rock. Their raw sound and fringe status, even with Bowie's patronage, appealed to those who embraced weirdness. "And this is how the first three Stooges albums became some of the most important templates for what would be eventually called punk rock."

podcast.title: The Stooges' Foundational Impact
podcast.body: The Stooges were deemed "absolutely bloody essential" in setting the stage for the punk movement that would define subsequent decades. "absolutely bloody essential in setting the stage for all the punk, alternative, and New Rock that was to come in the decades ahead."

podcast.title: Themes in Irish Punk
podcast.body: Irish punk bands tackled common themes of working-class life, politics, inheritance, identity, and drinking, contributing to the distinct sub-genre of Celtic punk. "Like most punk bands, they tackled themes of working-class life in politics, at inheritance, identity, and drinking, and basically you have Celtic punk."

podcast.title: Third Cycle Catalyst (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: Rising from the "streets of New York and London through 1976," punk rock was embraced by a new generation "fed up with the state of music" in the early 1970s, exploding in March 1977 and initiating rock's third cycle. "Punk rose from the streets of New York and London through 1976 before exploding in March of 1977 when the sex pistols tried to release God Save the Queen."

podcast.title: Tom Petty's Sound
podcast.body: Tom Petty's music, characterized as edgy rock and roll, was noted for sounding "a bit punk," even though Petty himself reportedly disliked that comparison. podcast.title: Toronto Scene
podcast.body: The punk scene in Toronto, while tiny, was significant enough to form the "third leg of a triangle that extended through both New York and London." It was not as artsy as New York punk, nor as political or class-conscious as UK punk, but it was characterized by its raw anger. "Toronto punk wasn't as artsy as New York punk. And it certainly wasn't as political or as class conscious as what they were doing in the UK. But man, it could still be really, really angry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Transatlantic Origin
podcast.body: The punk aesthetic did not originate in London as commonly believed, but rather in New York in the early 1970s with Richard Hell. Through a series of coincidences, this aesthetic idea traveled from one place to another and from one person to another, eventually becoming a global movement. "La verdad es que sale como de un sitio muy lejano de Londres y muy altrilados expuestos. Y las casualidades hicieron que esa idea estética fue se viajando de un lugar a otro y de una persona a otra hasta convertirse en un movimiento estético."

podcast.title: Transformative Impact
podcast.body: Punk music, pioneered by bands like the Ramones and Sex Pistols, drastically changed the music scene. Its influence led to the development of numerous new groups and genres, including alternative rock. "It started with bands like the Ramones and the Sex Pistols and Blondie."

podcast.title: Transition to Rock Sound
podcast.body: Billy Talent's first two albums were considered "punk records," but their third album, "Billy Talent 3," marked a shift towards a more "rock record" sound. This evolution was partly a conscious effort to move beyond the early 2000s "screamy" trend and incorporate more melody into their music. "it was kind of our rock record where the first two were more of a punk record."

podcast.title: UK Punk Rock Singles
podcast.body: "New Rose" by The Damned was the first-ever punk rock single released in the UK, followed by the Sex Pistols' "Anarchy in the UK" as the second, both released in 1976. "It was released on November 26th, 1976, and has gone down in history as the second ever punk rock single in the UK. Anybody know the first? Anyone? Song called New Rose by the Damned."

podcast.title: UK Scene's Political and Class-Conscious Nature
podcast.body: In contrast to the North American scene, punk rock in the UK, exemplified by bands like the Sex Pistols and The Clash, was intensely political and class-conscious. It focused heavily on challenging the establishment, criticizing the class system, and railing against the status quo. "But for the most parts, the North American punk scene was nowhere nearly as political or as class conscious as what we saw in the UK."

podcast.title: UK Terminology
podcast.body: In the UK, the term "alternative" did not gain traction, with "Indie" becoming the prevalent term due to the music predominantly originating from independent labels. Despite this, there is significant overlap between "Indie" and "alternative." "Meanwhile, in the UK, the word alternative never really caught on. Since most of this new music was coming from independent labels, the word Indy stuck."

podcast.title: UK Transformation
podcast.body: Upon reaching the UK, punk rock took on a distinct identity, intensely fueled by political grievances and the entrenched class system, contrasting with its more artistic New York counterpart. "In England though, things were rather different. English punk was very, very different from what was happening in America. Well, punk was more of an art statement in New York. It was fueled by politics and the class system in the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: UK vs. New York Styles
podcast.body: British punk was distinct from its New York counterpart. While American punk was described as "artsy, quoting French poets," UK punk was fueled by the stark realities of "inequities of the British class system, a failing economy, a crumbling empire, and a new generation of unemployed young people." "But British punk wasn't just a copy of what was happening in New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: UK vs. North American Political Stance
podcast.body: The UK punk scene, exemplified by bands like the Sex Pistols and The Clash, was significantly more political and class-conscious than its North American counterpart. It focused on challenging the establishment, the class system, and the status quo, which attracted attention from Eastern Bloc secret police organizations like the KGB. "for the most part, the North American punk scene was nowhere nearly as political or as class conscious as what we saw in the UK."

podcast.body: Punk was "first spawned in the States" but was "adopted early by the brits and arguably codified by UK-Aths," even though only a handful of first-wave punk artists had actual chart hits. podcast.title: Victorian Era Slang
podcast.body: By the Victorian era, "punk" had evolved into a slang word with dual meanings: either a type of Chinese incense or a derogatory term for someone or something perceived as of poor quality or utterly worthless. "By the Victorian era, a punk was a slang word that described either a type of Chinese incense or someone or something who was of poor quality or downright worthless."

podcast.title: Vinyl Adherence (Post-CD Era)
podcast.body: Punk bands, along with other alt-rock groups, were noted for their refusal to adopt digital music, consistently releasing 7-inch singles and vinyl albums through independent record stores. "Punk and other alt-rock bands. There were many groups who never bought into digital ever."

podcast.title: Waning Influence (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: By 1979, the punk movement, which had seen a massive wave in 1977, was described as "dying." This decline created an opportune moment for bands like Joy Division to forge new, more reflective and atmospheric sounds, making the decision to move beyond punk an intelligent and successful one. "fue una decisión como muy inteligente y muy acertada salirse de un pan que estaba muriendo para entrar en ese terreno."

podcast.title: Warped Tour Focus
podcast.body: The Warped Tour, created by Kevin Lyman, was primarily focused on punk music when it started in 1995, though it eventually branched out into other genres like hip-hop. "Warped was primarily about punk, but eventually it branched out into different genres like hip-hop."

podcast.title: Warped Tour Sponsorship Acceptance
podcast.body: Despite the anti-establishment and "left leaning tendencies" of many indie and punk bands featured on the Warped Tour, the consistent underwriting by Vans, a shoe company, was largely accepted by fans. This was attributed to Vans being perceived as "cool" by the demographic, and the sponsorship helping to keep ticket prices low, allowing the expensive tour to operate. "But because vans are considered cool by that crowd there wasn't too much squawking about it despite the politics and left leaning tendencies of many of the acts that played."

podcast.body: In the early 1980s, conventional wisdom on the West Coast was that punk was "over" and had been a mere "fad." This perception led to a widespread disinterest among record labels in signing punk bands, even highly regarded ones like Black Flag. "Conventional West Coast wisdom was the punk was over."
